notes.front: In aircraft metals, what is hardness?
notes.explanation: Cold-working raises it, and so does heat-treatment for steel and certain aluminium alloys.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Hardness”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Hardness refers to the ability of a material to resist abrasion, penetration, cutting action, or permanent distortion. Hardness may be increased by cold-working the metal and, in the case of steel and certain aluminum alloys, by heat-treatment.
notes.back: The ability of a material to resist abrasion, penetration, cutting action or permanent distortion.
notes.example: Like a structural bracket bent to shape while the metal is soft, then heat-treated so it keeps that shape.

notes.front: In aircraft metals, what is strength?
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that the type of load or stress on the material affects the strength it shows, and that hardness and strength are closely associated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Strength”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Strength is the ability of a material to resist deformation. Strength is also the ability of a material to resist stress without breaking. The type of load or stress on the material affects the strength it exhibits.
notes.back: The ability of a material to resist deformation, and to resist stress without breaking.
notes.example: Like a fitting that carries its load without bending out of shape; the same metal may show different strength in tension and in shear.

notes.front: What is malleability in a metal?
notes.explanation: Sheet metal worked into curved shapes such as cowlings, fairings or wingtips needs this property.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Malleability”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: A metal that can be hammered, rolled, or pressed into various shapes without cracking, breaking, or leaving some other detrimental effect, is said to be malleable. This property is necessary in sheet metal that is worked into curved shapes, such as cowlings, fairings, or wingtips.
notes.back: The property that lets a metal be hammered, rolled or pressed into shape without cracking, breaking or other harmful effect.
notes.example: Copper is the handbook’s example of a malleable metal.

notes.front: What is ductility in a metal?
notes.explanation: Wire and tubing depend on it, and ductile metals are preferred in aircraft for easy forming and resistance to failure under shock loads.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Ductility”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Ductility is the property of a metal that permits it to be permanently drawn, bent, or twisted into various shapes without breaking. This property is essential for metals used in making wire and tubing. Ductile metals are greatly preferred for aircraft use because of their ease of forming and resistance to failure under shock loads.
notes.back: The property that lets a metal be permanently drawn, bent or twisted into shape without breaking.
notes.example: Aluminium alloys used for fuselage and wing skin and for formed or extruded ribs, spars and bulkheads.

notes.front: What is elasticity in a metal?
notes.explanation: A part permanently distorted after its load was removed would be highly undesirable, which is why the property is so valuable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Elasticity”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Elasticity is a property that enables a metal to return to its original size and shape when the force that causes the change of shape is removed. This property is extremely valuable, because it would be highly undesirable to have a part permanently distorted after an applied load was removed.
notes.back: The property that lets a metal return to its original size and shape once the force that changed its shape is removed.
notes.example: Spring steel, which the handbook names as having this property.

notes.front: What is toughness in a metal?
notes.explanation: The handbook calls toughness a desirable property in aircraft metals; it is the opposite behaviour to a brittle metal that cracks without changing shape.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Toughness”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: A material that possesses toughness withstands tearing or shearing and may be stretched or otherwise deformed without breaking. Toughness is a desirable property in aircraft metals.
notes.back: The property of withstanding tearing or shearing, and being stretched or otherwise deformed without breaking.
notes.example: Like a skin panel that stretches and dents under an overload instead of tearing apart.

notes.front: What is brittleness in a metal?
notes.explanation: Structural metals often meet shock loads, so the handbook says brittleness is not a very desirable property.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Brittleness”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Brittleness is the property of a metal that allows little bending or deformation without shattering. A brittle metal is apt to break or crack without change of shape. Because structural metals are often subjected to shock loads, brittleness is not a
notes.back: The property that allows little bending or deformation before shattering; a brittle metal tends to break or crack without changing shape.
notes.example: Cast iron, cast aluminium and very hard steel are the handbook’s examples.

notes.front: What is fusibility?
notes.explanation: Welding fuses metals, so fusibility matters there: steels fuse around 2,600 °F and aluminium alloys at approximately 1,100 °F.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Fusibility”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: Fusibility is the ability of a metal to become liquid by the application of heat. Metals are fused in welding. Steels fuse around 2,600 °F and aluminum alloys at approximately 1,100 °F.
notes.back: The ability of a metal to become liquid when heat is applied.
notes.example: Like the edges of two steel tubes melting and flowing together into one piece during welding.

notes.front: What is conductivity in a metal?
notes.explanation: Heat conductivity governs how much heat welding needs for proper fusion; electrical conductivity matters for bonding to eliminate radio interference.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Conductivity”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: Conductivity is the property that enables a metal to carry heat or electricity. The heat conductivity of a metal is especially important in welding, because it governs the amount of heat that is required for proper fusion.
notes.back: The property that lets a metal carry heat or electricity.
notes.example: Like choosing a welding jig: the metal’s conductivity partly decides which jig is used to control expansion and contraction.

notes.front: What is SAE steel numbering?
notes.explanation: Four numerals designate plain carbon and alloy steels, five some alloy steels, so the number tells the steel type and its carbon range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Steel and Steel Alloys”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: A numerical index, sponsored by the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) and the American Iron and Steel Institute (AISI), is used to identify the chemical compositions of the structural steels. In this system, a four-numeral series is used to designate the plain carbon and alloy steels;
notes.back: A numerical index sponsored by the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) and another institute that identifies the chemical composition of structural steels.
notes.example: SAE 1025: the 10 marks a non-sulphurised carbon steel, and the last two digits point to the middle of its carbon range.

notes.front: What is the aluminium alloy designation system for wrought alloys?
notes.explanation: The digits identify the alloy type, its modifications and the particular alloy, so a number such as 2024 describes the metal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: Wrought aluminum and wrought aluminum alloys are designated by a four-digit index system. The system is broken into three distinct groups: 1xxx group, 2xxx through 8xxx group, and 9xxx group (which is currently unused).
notes.back: A four-digit index in three groups: 1xxx, 2xxx to 8xxx, and 9xxx (currently unused).
notes.example: 2024: the first digit, 2, marks copper as the main alloying element.

notes.front: What is Alclad?
notes.explanation: The pure coating protects the core twice: it keeps corrosive agents off and protects the core electrolytically.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Alclad Aluminum”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: The terms “Alclad and Pureclad” are used to designate sheets that consist of an aluminum-alloy core coated with a layer of pure aluminum to a depth of approximately 51⁄2 percent on each side. The pure aluminum coating affords a dual protection for the core, preventing contact with any corrosive agents, and protecting the core electrolytically
notes.back: Sheet with an aluminium-alloy core coated on each side with pure aluminium, to a depth of about 5½ percent.
notes.example: Clad sheet dipped in caustic soda stays bright on the surface but shows a dark area in the middle when viewed from the edge.

notes.front: What is a magnesium alloy, as the handbook describes it?
notes.explanation: Pure magnesium lacks the strength for structural use, and it weighs only two-thirds as much as aluminium.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Magnesium & Magnesium Alloys”, p. 7-8
notes.evidence: Magnesium, the world’s lightest structural metal, is a silvery white material weighing only two-thirds as much as aluminum. Magnesium does not possess sufficient strength in its pure state for structural uses, but when alloyed with zinc, aluminum, and manganese, it produces an alloy having the highest strengthto-weight ratio of any of the commonly used metals.
notes.back: Magnesium alloyed with zinc, aluminium and manganese: the highest strength-to-weight ratio of the commonly used metals.
notes.example: Nosewheel doors, flap cover skin and engine nacelles have been made of it to save weight.

notes.front: Where does titanium sit among aircraft metals?
notes.explanation: It also has low thermal conductivity, a low coefficient of expansion and a melting point from 2,730 °F to 3,155 °F.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Titanium and Titanium Alloys”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: Titanium falls between aluminum and stainless steel in terms of elasticity, density, and elevated temperature strength. It has a melting point from 2,730 °F to 3,155 °F, low thermal conductivity, and a low coefficient of expansion. It is light, strong, and resistant to stress corrosion cracking.
notes.back: Between aluminium and stainless steel in elasticity, density and elevated-temperature strength; light, strong and resistant to stress corrosion cracking.
notes.example: Compressor disks, blades and vanes in turbine engines, and firewalls in airframes.

notes.front: What is a copper alloy, and what is copper itself used for in aircraft?
notes.explanation: The handbook singles out beryllium copper as one of the most successful copper-base alloys.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Copper and Copper Alloys”, p. 7-10
notes.evidence: In aircraft, copper is used primarily in the electrical system for bus bars, bonding, and as lock wire. Beryllium copper is one of the most successful of all the copper base alloys.
notes.back: An alloy with copper as its base, such as beryllium copper; copper itself goes mainly into electrical bus bars, bonding and lock wire.
notes.example: Beryllium copper: about 97 percent copper and 2 percent beryllium, used for diaphragms, precision bearings and spring washers.

notes.front: Which two nickel alloys are used in aircraft?
notes.explanation: Monel is mostly nickel with a large share of copper, plus small amounts of iron and manganese.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Nickel & Nickel Alloys”, p. 7-11
notes.evidence: There are basically two nickel alloys used in aircraft: Monel and Inconel. Monel contains about 68 percent nickel and 29 percent copper, plus small amounts of iron and manganese.
notes.back: Monel and Inconel.
notes.example: Inconel in turbine engines; Monel in exhaust manifolds and carburettor needle valves.

notes.front: What is forging?
notes.explanation: The recrystallisation temperature is the dividing line the handbook uses between cold and hot forging.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Forging”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: Forging is the process of forming a product by hammering or pressing. When the material is forged below the recrystallization temperature, it is called cold forged. When worked above the recrystallization temperature, it is referred
notes.back: Forming a product by hammering or pressing: cold forged below the recrystallisation temperature, hot forged above it.
notes.example: Drop forging: a hot ingot between formed dies under a drop hammer, with a weight of several tons dropped on the upper die.

notes.front: What is casting?
notes.explanation: No plastic deformation happens, so the grain shape and orientation cannot be altered as they are in worked metal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Casting”, p. 7-28
notes.evidence: Melting the metal and pouring it into a mold of the desired shape forms casting. Since plastic deformation of the metal does not occur, no alteration of the grain shape or orientation is possible.
notes.back: Melting metal and pouring it into a mould of the desired shape.
notes.example: Turbine blades with internal passages, where casting may be the most economical process.

notes.front: What is extrusion?
notes.explanation: The die opening becomes the cross-section of the finished piece, such as an angle, channel or tube.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Extruding”, p. 7-28
notes.evidence: The extrusion process involves the forcing of metal through an opening in a die, thus causing the metal to take the shape of the die opening. The shape of the die will be the cross section of an angle, channel, tube, or some other shape.
notes.back: Forcing metal through an opening in a die so that it takes the shape of the opening.
notes.example: Aluminium channels, angles, T-sections and Z-sections pushed out by a hydraulic ram.

notes.front: What is heat treatment?
notes.explanation: The aim is a metal that is more useful, serviceable and safe for a definite purpose.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-treatment”, p. 7-13
notes.evidence: Heat-treatment is a series of operations involving the heating and cooling of metals in the solid state. Its purpose is to change a mechanical property, or combination of mechanical properties, so that the metal is more useful, serviceable, and safe for a definite purpose.
notes.back: A series of operations heating and cooling a metal in the solid state to change a mechanical property.
notes.example: Hardening a steel part makes it harder and stronger, but the handbook warns a hardened metal may become brittle.

notes.front: What is tempering?
notes.explanation: Tempering always follows hardening, never precedes it, and it also softens the steel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Tempering”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Tempering reduces the brittleness imparted by hardening and produces definite physical properties within the steel. Tempering always follows, never precedes, the hardening operation. In addition to reducing brittleness, tempering softens the steel.
notes.back: Reheating hardened steel to reduce the brittleness hardening imparted and give it definite physical properties.
notes.example: A steel fitting quenched hard, then reheated to a chosen temperature to reach a set tensile strength.

notes.front: What does annealing do to steel?
notes.explanation: In the annealed state steel has its lowest strength; the handbook calls annealing, in general, the opposite of hardening.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Annealing”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Annealing of steel produces a fine-grained, soft, ductile metal without internal stresses or strains. In the annealed state, steel has its lowest strength. In general, annealing is the opposite of hardening.
notes.back: Produces a fine-grained, soft, ductile metal without internal stresses or strains.
notes.example: A part heated just above the upper critical point, soaked, then left to cool very slowly in the furnace.

notes.front: What does normalising do to steel?
notes.explanation: Uncontrolled stress leads to failure; aircraft steels are often used normalised, but seldom if ever annealed, because of the better physical properties.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Normalizing”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: The normalizing of steel removes the internal stresses set up by heat-treating, welding, casting, forming, or machining. Stress, if not controlled, leads to failure. Because of the better physical properties, aircraft steels are often used in the normalized state, but seldom, if ever, in the annealed state.
notes.back: Removes the internal stresses set up by heat-treating, welding, casting, forming or machining.
notes.example: A welded engine mount heated above the upper critical point and cooled in still air after fabrication.

notes.front: What does case hardening produce?
notes.explanation: It suits parts that need a wear-resistant surface yet must be tough enough inside to carry the applied loads.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Case Hardening”, p. 7-20
notes.evidence: Case hardening produces a hard, wear-resistant surface or case over a strong, tough core. Case hardening is ideal for parts that require a wear-resistant surface and, at the same time, must be tough enough internally to withstand the applied loads.
notes.back: A hard, wear-resistant surface (the case) over a strong, tough core.
notes.example: Carburising adds carbon to the surface of low-carbon steel; nitriding forms iron nitride at the surface.

notes.front: What is solution heat-treatment of aluminium?
notes.explanation: Ageing, the fourth step, comes afterwards, either naturally at room temperature or artificially.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: The hardening of an aluminum alloy by heat-treatment consists of four distinct steps: The first three steps above are known as solution heat-treatment, although it has become common practice to use the shorter term, “heat-treatment.”
notes.back: The first three of the four steps in hardening an aluminium alloy by heat-treatment, often just called “heat-treatment”.
notes.example: A 2024 sheet heated, soaked and quenched in cold water, then left to age at room temperature.

notes.front: What is precipitation heat-treatment?
notes.explanation: It is the artificial counterpart of natural ageing, which happens at room temperature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: Room temperature hardening is known as natural aging, while hardening done at moderate temperatures is called artificial aging, or precipitation heat-treatment.
notes.back: Hardening an aluminium alloy at moderate temperatures after solution treatment; also called artificial ageing.
notes.example: A 7075 part solution heat-treated, then held at a moderate oven temperature for many hours.

notes.front: What is an icebox rivet?
notes.explanation: They give more strength than a same-size 2117-T field rivet (the handbook prints “2217-T” here), but age harden at room temperature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Solid Shank Rivets”, p. 7-52
notes.evidence: The 2017-T and 2024-T rivets are used in aluminum-alloy structures where more strength is needed than is obtainable with the same size 2217-T rivet. These rivets are known as “ice box rivets,” are annealed and must be kept refrigerated until they are to be driven.
notes.back: A 2017-T or 2024-T rivet, annealed and kept refrigerated until it is driven.
notes.example: A tray of 2024-T rivets taken from the shop refrigerator just before a structural repair.

notes.front: How much wood is used in aircraft construction today?
notes.explanation: The earliest aircraft were built of wood and cloth, but wood is now rare in construction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wood”, p. 7-29
notes.evidence: The earliest aircraft were constructed of wood and cloth. Today, except for restorations and some home-built aircraft, very little wood is used in aircraft construction.
notes.back: Very little, except for restorations and some home-built aircraft.
notes.example: Like a vintage biplane being restored with a new wooden spar.

notes.front: Into which two classes are aircraft transparent plastics divided?
notes.explanation: The two classes are defined by how each reacts to heat.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Transparent Plastics”, p. 7-29
notes.evidence: Transparent plastic materials used in aircraft canopies, such as windshields, windows and other similar transparent enclosures, may be divided into two major classes or groups: thermoplastic and thermosetting. These plastics are classified according to their reaction to heat.
notes.back: Thermoplastic and thermosetting, classified by their reaction to heat.
notes.example: Windshields, windows and canopies; a newer material is stretched acrylic.

notes.front: What is a composite material?
notes.explanation: Any of the three reinforcement forms, fibre, whisker or particle, works as long as a resin holds it in place.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Composite Materials”, p. 7-30
notes.evidence: the composition of composite materials is a combination of reinforcement, such as a fiber, whisker, or particle, surrounded and held in place by a resin forming a structure.
notes.back: Reinforcement such as a fibre, whisker or particle, surrounded and held in place by a resin to form a structure.
notes.example: The handbook’s example is concrete: cement as the resin, gravel or reinforcing rods as the reinforcement.

notes.front: What is a bungee cord?
notes.explanation: Type II is quickly replaced and need not be secured by stretching and whipping.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Shock Absorber Cord”, p. 7-33
notes.evidence: There are two types of elastic shock absorbing cord. Type I is a straight cord, and type II is a continuous ring known as a “bungee.” The advantages of the type II cord are that it is easily and quickly replaced and does not need to be secured by stretching and whipping.
notes.back: Type II shock absorber cord: a continuous ring. Type I is a straight cord.
notes.example: A ring of shock cord looped around a landing gear leg; the cord is natural rubber strands in a braided cotton cover.

notes.front: What is an O-ring packing?
notes.explanation: Because it seals both ways it is the most commonly used type of packing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “O-Ring Packings”, p. 7-34
notes.evidence: O-ring packings are used to prevent both internal and external leakage. This type of packing ring seals effectively in both directions and is the type most commonly used.
notes.back: A packing ring that prevents internal and external leakage and seals effectively in both directions.
notes.example: The seal on a hydraulic actuating cylinder piston, with backup rings where pressure is high.

notes.front: What is an AN bolt?
notes.explanation: The all-purpose hex head bolt suits general applications where a light drive fit is allowed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “General Purpose Bolts”, p. 7-37
notes.evidence: The hex head aircraft bolt (AN-3 through AN-20) is an all-purpose structural bolt used for general applications involving tension or shear loads where a light drive fit is permissible
notes.back: An Air Force-Navy (AN) standard aircraft bolt; the hex head AN-3 to AN-20 is the all-purpose structural bolt.
notes.example: A general purpose hex head AN bolt holding a steel fitting to a wing rib.

notes.front: What is a close tolerance bolt?
notes.explanation: A tight drive fit means the bolt moves into position only when struck with a 12- to 14-ounce hammer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Close Tolerance Bolts”, p. 7-38
notes.evidence: Close tolerance bolts are machined more accurately than the general-purpose bolt. Close tolerance bolts may be hex headed (AN-173 through AN-186) or have a 100° countersunk head (NAS-80 through NAS-86). They are used in applications where a tight drive fit is required. (The bolt moves into position only when struck with a 12- to 14-ounce hammer.)
notes.back: A bolt machined more accurately than the general purpose bolt, used where a tight drive fit is required.
notes.example: A countersunk-head close tolerance bolt in a reamed fitting hole on a wing attachment.

notes.front: What are internal wrenching bolts?
notes.explanation: Standard AN hex head bolts and washers lack the strength to replace them, so only another internal wrenching bolt will do.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Internal Wrenching Bolts”, p. 7-38
notes.evidence: Replace an internal wrenching bolt with another internal wrenching bolt. Standard AN hex head bolts and washers cannot be substituted for them, as they do not have the required strength.
notes.back: High-strength steel bolts with a recessed head for an internal wrench, suitable for tension and shear.
notes.example: In steel parts the hole is slightly countersunk for the shank radius; in Dural, a special heat-treated washer is used under the head.

notes.front: What is a solid shank rivet?
notes.explanation: They are the rivets generally used in repair work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Solid Shank Rivets”, p. 7-52
notes.evidence: Solid shank rivets are generally used in repair work. They are identified by the kind of material of which they are made, their head type, size of shank, and their temper condition.
notes.back: The common aircraft rivet, driven with a bucking bar; identified by material, head type, shank size and temper.
notes.example: A universal head aluminium-alloy rivet joining a skin patch, its shop head formed with a bucking bar.

notes.front: What is a turnlock fastener?
notes.explanation: Its most desirable feature is quick and easy removal of access panels for inspection and servicing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Turn Lock Fasteners”, p. 7-64
notes.evidence: also referred to by such terms as quick opening, quick action, and stressed panel fasteners. The most desirable feature of these fasteners is that they permit quick and easy removal of access panels for inspection and servicing purposes.
notes.back: A fastener that secures inspection plates, doors and other removable panels; also called quick opening, quick action or stressed panel fastener.
notes.example: A cowling held by fasteners that lock with a quarter turn of a screwdriver.

notes.front: What is a nut plate?
notes.explanation: Being permanently mounted, nut plates let inspection panels and access doors be removed and installed easily.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Nut Plates”, p. 7-68
notes.evidence: Nuts that are made to be riveted in place in aircraft are called nut plates. Their purpose is to allow bolts and screws to be inserted without having to hold the nut. They are permanently mounted to enable inspection panels and access doors to be easily removed and installed.
notes.back: A nut made to be riveted in place, so bolts and screws can be inserted without holding the nut.
notes.example: Floating anchor nuts behind a floor panel, free to move so each screw lines up easily.

notes.front: What is a control cable, and where is it used?
notes.explanation: It is strong and lightweight, and its flexibility makes it easy to route through the aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Control Cables & Terminals”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: Cables are the most widely used linkage in primary flight control systems. Cable-type linkage is also used in engine controls, emergency extension systems for the landing gear, and various other systems throughout the aircraft. Cable-type linkage has several advantages over the other types. It is strong and lightweight, and its flexibility makes it easy to route through the aircraft.
notes.back: A steel wire-strand linkage; the most widely used linkage in primary flight control systems.
notes.example: Cables running over pulleys from the control column to the elevator.

notes.front: What is push-pull tube linkage?
notes.explanation: One tube can both push and pull, which removes the problem of varying tension.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Push-Pull Tube Linkage”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: This type linkage eliminates the problem of varying tension and permits the transfer of either compression or tension stress through a single tube.
notes.back: A hollow aluminium-alloy or steel tube with adjustable end fittings, carrying compression or tension through one tube.
notes.example: A short tube connecting a bellcrank to an aileron horn.

notes.front: What is safety wire, as a safetying method?
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it the most positive and satisfactory way to safety parts that cannot be safetied by any other practical means.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Safety Wiring”, p. 7-77
notes.evidence: Safety wiring is the most positive and satisfactory method of safetying cap screws, studs, nuts, bolt heads, and turnbuckle barrels, which cannot be safetied by any other practical means. It is a method of wiring together two or more units in such a manner that any tendency of one to loosen is counteracted by the tightening of the wire.
notes.back: Wire joining two or more units so any tendency of one to loosen is counteracted by the tightening of the wire.
notes.example: Two drilled-head bolts wired together so that if either starts to turn loose, the wire pulls it tight.

notes.front: What is a turnbuckle?
notes.explanation: Fitted into the cable run, it lets length and tension be trimmed without changing the cable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Turnbuckles”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: A turnbuckle assembly is a mechanical screw device consisting of two threaded terminals and a threaded barrel. [Figure 7-70] Turnbuckles are fitted in the cable assembly for making minor adjustments in cable length and for adjusting cable tension.
notes.back: A mechanical screw device of two threaded terminals and a threaded barrel, for minor cable-length and tension adjustments.
notes.example: The barrel in a rudder cable run, turned to set the cable tension and then safetied.

notes.front: What is a snap ring?
notes.explanation: Tempering gives the metal its spring, and that spring is what grips the groove.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Snap Rings”, p. 7-80
notes.evidence: A snap ring is a ring of metal, either round or flat in cross section, which is tempered to have spring like action. This spring like action holds the snap ring firmly seated in a groove.
notes.back: A round or flat metal ring tempered to spring action, which holds it firmly seated in a groove.
notes.example: A ring sprung into a groove on a shaft with special pliers to keep a part from sliding off.

notes.front: What is brazing?
notes.explanation: The base metal itself is not melted, which is the difference from welding.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-74b, p. 4-63
notes.evidence: Brazing is similar to welding in that heat is used to join the material; but rather than melting, the metal is heated only enough to melt a brazing rod having a much lower melting point.
notes.back: Joining metals by heating them only enough to melt a filler rod with a much lower melting point.
notes.example: Silver brazing a high-pressure oxygen line fitting.

notes.front: What is solder?
notes.explanation: Soldering works like brazing, so the temperature at which the filler melts is what separates the two.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-74c, p. 4-63
notes.evidence: Soldering is similar to brazing except that brazing materials normally melt at temperatures above 425 ºC (800 °F), while solders melt at temperatures considerably lower.
notes.back: A filler that melts at temperatures considerably lower than brazing materials, which normally melt above 800 °F.
notes.example: Half-and-half tin-lead solder joining an electrical connection.

notes.front: What are the hardware identification tables in Advisory Circular 43.13-1B?
notes.explanation: The tables are keyed to paragraph 7-195 of the circular.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, ch. 7, section 11, p. 7-54
notes.evidence: SECTION 11. HARDWARE IDENTIFICATION TABLES TABLE 7-10. TABLE OF RIVETS Par 7-195
notes.back: Section 11 of its chapter 7: tables that identify aircraft hardware, starting with Table 7-10, the table of rivets.
notes.example: Looking up a rivet’s standard number in Table 7-10 to confirm its head style.

notes.front: What is a suspected unapproved part (SUP)?
notes.explanation: Such parts may not be approved, so the handbook tells technicians to raise the concern with a foreman, supervisor or quality person.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 2, “Suspected Unapproved Parts (SUP)”, p. 2-24
notes.evidence: The center two categories of parts represent suspected unapproved parts. If either the physical part or the paperwork associated with the part is questionable, it is best to contact the shop foreman, shift supervisor, or the assigned quality individual to discuss your concerns.
notes.back: A part whose physical part or paperwork is questionable: a good part with bad paperwork, or a bad part with “good” (bogus) paperwork.
notes.example: A new-looking bolt that arrives with a certificate that does not match its part number.

notes.front: How do the certification standards treat personal protective equipment (PPE) in this area?
notes.explanation: The standards list it as the first risk-management element for this area, beside improper torque and suspected unapproved parts.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant ACS (FAA-S-ACS-1), I.E Aircraft Materials, Hardware, and Processes, p. 7
notes.evidence: The applicant demonstrates the ability to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with: AM.I.E.R1 Use of personal protective equipment (PPE).
notes.back: Use of personal protective equipment (PPE) is a risk the applicant must identify, assess and mitigate for materials, hardware and processes.
notes.example: For composite work the handbook calls for a respirator, leak-proof goggles, and gloves or barrier creams.

notes.front: A technician checks whether a heat-treated part resists a penetrator being pressed into its surface. Which property is being judged?
notes.explanation: Resisting penetration is part of the definition of hardness, and hardness testers measure resistance to penetration.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Hardness”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Hardness refers to the ability of a material to resist abrasion, penetration, cutting action, or permanent distortion.
notes.back: B) Hardness
notes.choices:
A) Ductility
B) Hardness
C) Fusibility
D) Conductivity
notes.choicesExplained: A: ductility is being drawn or bent permanently without breaking, not resisting penetration. C: fusibility is becoming liquid under heat. D: conductivity is carrying heat or electricity.

notes.front: How is the tensile strength of a material worked out, and in what unit?
notes.explanation: Tensile strength is the material’s resistance to a force tending to pull it apart, so it is expressed per unit of area.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Strength”, p. 7-13
notes.evidence: Tensile strength is measured in pounds per square inch (psi) and is calculated by dividing the load in pounds required to pull the material apart by its cross-sectional area in square inches.
notes.back: The load in pounds needed to pull it apart, divided by its cross-sectional area in square inches: pounds per square inch (psi).

notes.front: A test bar with a cross-section of 0.5 square inch pulls apart at 30,000 pounds. What is its tensile strength?
notes.explanation: Dividing the breaking load by the cross-sectional area gives the strength per square inch: 30,000 ÷ 0.5.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Strength”, p. 7-13
notes.evidence: Tensile strength is measured in pounds per square inch (psi) and is calculated by dividing the load in pounds required to pull the material apart by its cross-sectional area in square inches.
notes.choicesExplained: A: this multiplies the load by the area instead of dividing by it. B: this is the breaking load in pounds, not the load per square inch. D: this misplaces the decimal: 30,000 ÷ 0.5 is 60,000.

notes.front: A shop must hammer a sheet into a curved wingtip fairing without it cracking. Which property of the sheet matters most?
notes.explanation: The handbook says malleability is necessary in sheet metal worked into curved shapes such as wingtips.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Malleability”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: This property is necessary in sheet metal that is worked into curved shapes, such as cowlings, fairings, or wingtips.
notes.back: D) Malleability
notes.choices:
A) Brittleness
B) Fusibility
C) Conductivity
D) Malleability
notes.choicesExplained: A: a brittle metal cracks with little deformation, the opposite of what is needed. B: fusibility is about melting, which plays no part in hammering a sheet to shape. C: conductivity is about carrying heat or electricity.

notes.front: A metal is to be drawn into tubing and must also resist failure under shock loads. Which property should it have?
notes.explanation: Ductility is essential for wire and tubing, and ductile metals resist failure under shock loads.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Ductility”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: This property is essential for metals used in making wire and tubing. Ductile metals are greatly preferred for aircraft use because of their ease of forming and resistance to failure under shock loads.
notes.back: D) Ductility
notes.choices:
A) Brittleness
B) Hardness
C) Fusibility
D) Ductility
notes.choicesExplained: A: brittle metals shatter under shock loads rather than resisting them. B: hardness is resistance to penetration and wear, not the ability to be drawn into tube. C: fusibility concerns melting, not forming.

notes.front: Aircraft members are designed so that their maximum loads never stress them beyond their {{c1::elastic limit}}.
notes.explanation: Loading a metal past this point causes permanent distortion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Elasticity”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Each metal has a point known as the elastic limit, beyond which it cannot be loaded without causing permanent distortion. In aircraft construction, members and parts are so designed that the maximum loads to which they are subjected do not stress them beyond their elastic limits.

notes.front: After a heavy landing, a gear spring leg stays slightly bent even though the load has gone. What has happened?
notes.explanation: Loading a metal beyond its elastic limit causes permanent distortion instead of a return to the original shape.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Elasticity”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Each metal has a point known as the elastic limit, beyond which it cannot be loaded without causing permanent distortion.
notes.back: C) It was loaded beyond its elastic limit
notes.choices:
A) It became more ductile
B) It showed normal elasticity
C) It was loaded beyond its elastic limit
D) It was fused by the landing loads
notes.choicesExplained: B: elasticity means returning to the original shape, which the leg did not do. A: ductility is the ability to be formed without breaking, not a result of overload. D: fusion is melting by heat, which a landing does not cause.

notes.front: A casting cracks straight through under a sudden shock load, with no bending first. Which property does this show?
notes.explanation: A brittle metal breaks or cracks without change of shape, and cast metals are among the handbook’s examples.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Brittleness”, p. 7-1
notes.evidence: Brittleness is the property of a metal that allows little bending or deformation without shattering. A brittle metal is apt to break or crack without change of shape.
notes.back: A) Brittleness
notes.choices:
A) Brittleness
B) Toughness
C) Elasticity
D) Malleability
notes.choicesExplained: B: a tough metal stretches or deforms without breaking. C: elasticity is returning to shape after a load, not cracking. D: a malleable metal can be hammered or pressed without cracking.

notes.front: How do ferrous and nonferrous metals differ, and which test separates many of them?
notes.explanation: Each ferrous metal throws its own spark pattern, which is why the spark test works for them and not for most nonferrous metals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Ferrous Aircraft Metals”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: Each ferrous metal has its own peculiar spark characteristics. The spark streams vary from a few tiny shafts to a shower of sparks several feet in length. (Few nonferrous metals give off sparks when touched to a grinding stone. Therefore, these metals cannot be successfully identified by the spark test.)
notes.back: Ferrous metals have iron as their base; nonferrous do not. Few nonferrous metals spark on a grinding stone, so spark testing identifies ferrous ones.

notes.front: A mechanic touches an unknown bar to a grinding stone and it gives off almost no sparks. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
notes.explanation: Few nonferrous metals spark on a grinding stone, so they cannot be identified this way.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Ferrous Aircraft Metals”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: (Few nonferrous metals give off sparks when touched to a grinding stone. Therefore, these metals cannot be successfully identified by the spark test.)
notes.back: B) It is probably nonferrous, and the spark test cannot identify it
notes.choices:
A) It is low carbon steel
B) It is probably nonferrous, and the spark test cannot identify it
C) It is cast iron
D) It is high carbon steel
notes.choicesExplained: A: low carbon steels give long, straight shafts with a few white sprigs. C: cast iron gives red sparks that turn straw colour. D: more carbon gives more sprigs and a whiter stream, not an absence of sparks.

notes.front: In SAE steel numbering, the last two (or three) digits are intended to indicate the approximate middle of the {{c1::carbon range}}.
notes.explanation: The first two digits give the type of steel, so the number carries both the family and the carbon content.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Steel and Steel Alloys”, p. 7-2
notes.evidence: The first two digits indicate the type of steel, the second digit also generally (but not always) gives the approximate amount of the major alloying element, and the last two (or three) digits are intended to indicate the approximate middle of the carbon range.

notes.front: What carbon content, and which SAE numbers, make a low carbon steel?
notes.explanation: Steels of this grade make items such as safety wire, certain nuts, cable bushings and threaded rod ends.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Types, Characteristics, and Uses of Alloyed Steels”, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: Steel containing carbon in percentages ranging from 0.10 to 0.30 percent is classed as low carbon steel. The equivalent SAE numbers range from 1010 to 1030. Steels of this grade are used for making items, such as safety wire, certain nuts, cable bushings, or threaded rod ends.
notes.back: 0.10 to 0.30 percent carbon; SAE 1010 to 1030.

notes.front: A welded steel-tube fuselage needs repair tubing. Which steel family has practically replaced carbon steel for fuselage tubing and engine mounts?
notes.explanation: Molybdenum steels are especially adaptable for welding, so they are used mainly for welded structural parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Types, Characteristics, and Uses of Alloyed Steels”, p. 7-3
notes.evidence: They are especially adaptable for welding and, for this reason, are used principally for welded structural parts and assemblies. This type steel has practically replaced carbon steel in the fabrication of fuselage tubing, engine mounts, landing gears, and other structural parts.
notes.back: B) Chrome-molybdenum steel, such as SAE 4130
notes.choices:
A) Low carbon steel, SAE 1010 to 1030
B) Chrome-molybdenum steel, such as SAE 4130
C) Chrome-vanadium steel, SAE 6150
D) High carbon steel, SAE 1095
notes.choicesExplained: A: this is what chrome-molybdenum steel has practically replaced for such parts. D: this is used for flat and coil springs and has limited aircraft use. C: the handbook gives this for springs.

notes.front: In the electrochemical test that separates Inconel from stainless steel, what spot colours does each give?
notes.explanation: The test works by detecting nickel in the alloy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Electrochemical Test”, p. 7-5
notes.evidence: A bright, distinctly pink spot will appear within seconds on the filter paper if the metal being tested is Inconel. A brown spot will appear if the test metal is stainless steel.
notes.back: Inconel: a bright, distinctly pink spot. Stainless steel: a brown spot.

notes.front: In the 1xxx aluminium group, the last two digits give hundredths of 1 percent above 99 percent, so 1130 is {{c1::99.30}} percent pure aluminium.
notes.explanation: The first digit 1 already stands for 99 percent, and the last two digits add the hundredths.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: Thus, if the last two digits were 30, the alloy would contain 99 percent plus 0.30 percent of pure aluminum, or a total of 99.30 percent pure aluminum.

notes.front: In the wrought aluminium four-digit system, which major alloying element does a first digit of 2 (2xxx) indicate?
notes.explanation: Its best-known alloy is 2024; it has poor corrosion resistance unclad.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: In the 2xxx through 8xxx groups, the first digit indicates the major alloying element used in the formation of the alloy as follows: • 2xxx—copper • 3xxx—manganese • 4xxx—silicon • 5xxx—magnesium • 6xxx—magnesium and silicon • 7xxx—zinc • 8xxx—other elements
notes.back: Copper.

notes.front: In the wrought aluminium four-digit system, which major alloying element does a first digit of 3 (3xxx) indicate?
notes.explanation: The group is generally non-heat-treatable; 3003 is the most popular.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: In the 2xxx through 8xxx groups, the first digit indicates the major alloying element used in the formation of the alloy as follows: • 2xxx—copper • 3xxx—manganese • 4xxx—silicon • 5xxx—magnesium • 6xxx—magnesium and silicon • 7xxx—zinc • 8xxx—other elements
notes.back: Manganese.

notes.front: In the wrought aluminium four-digit system, which major alloying element does a first digit of 4 (4xxx) indicate?
notes.explanation: Silicon lowers melting temperature, and the group is used mainly in welding and brazing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: In the 2xxx through 8xxx groups, the first digit indicates the major alloying element used in the formation of the alloy as follows: • 2xxx—copper • 3xxx—manganese • 4xxx—silicon • 5xxx—magnesium • 6xxx—magnesium and silicon • 7xxx—zinc • 8xxx—other elements
notes.back: Silicon.

notes.front: In the wrought aluminium four-digit system, which major alloying element does a first digit of 5 (5xxx) indicate?
notes.explanation: The group has good welding and corrosion-resistant characteristics.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: In the 2xxx through 8xxx groups, the first digit indicates the major alloying element used in the formation of the alloy as follows: • 2xxx—copper • 3xxx—manganese • 4xxx—silicon • 5xxx—magnesium • 6xxx—magnesium and silicon • 7xxx—zinc • 8xxx—other elements
notes.back: Magnesium.

notes.front: In the wrought aluminium four-digit system, which major alloying element does a first digit of 6 (6xxx) indicate?
notes.explanation: Together they form magnesium silicide, which makes the alloys heat-treatable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: In the 2xxx through 8xxx groups, the first digit indicates the major alloying element used in the formation of the alloy as follows: • 2xxx—copper • 3xxx—manganese • 4xxx—silicon • 5xxx—magnesium • 6xxx—magnesium and silicon • 7xxx—zinc • 8xxx—other elements
notes.back: Magnesium and silicon.

notes.front: In the wrought aluminium four-digit system, which major alloying element does a first digit of 7 (7xxx) indicate?
notes.explanation: Its principal alloy is 7075, heat-treatable to very high strength.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: In the 2xxx through 8xxx groups, the first digit indicates the major alloying element used in the formation of the alloy as follows: • 2xxx—copper • 3xxx—manganese • 4xxx—silicon • 5xxx—magnesium • 6xxx—magnesium and silicon • 7xxx—zinc • 8xxx—other elements
notes.back: Zinc.

notes.front: In the wrought aluminium four-digit system, which major alloying element does a first digit of 8 (8xxx) indicate?
notes.explanation: Each other group names its main alloying element; 8xxx collects all other elements.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: In the 2xxx through 8xxx groups, the first digit indicates the major alloying element used in the formation of the alloy as follows: • 2xxx—copper • 3xxx—manganese • 4xxx—silicon • 5xxx—magnesium • 6xxx—magnesium and silicon • 7xxx—zinc • 8xxx—other elements
notes.back: Other elements.

notes.front: A repair drawing calls for a 5000-series sheet. What is its principal alloying element?
notes.explanation: The first digit of a wrought aluminium designation names the major alloying element, and 5 stands for magnesium.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: 5000 series: Magnesium is the principal alloying element. It has good welding and corrosion resistant characteristics.
notes.back: D) Magnesium
notes.choices:
A) Copper
B) Manganese
C) Zinc
D) Magnesium
notes.choicesExplained: B: manganese is the 3000 series. C: zinc is the 7000 series. A: copper is the 2000 series.

notes.front: In aluminium temper designations, what does the letter F after the alloy number mean?
notes.explanation: Metal “as fabricated” comes from the ingot without any controlled cold-working or thermal treatment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Hardness Identification”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: These designations are as follows: • F—as fabricated • O—annealed, recrystallized (wrought products only) • H—strain hardened
notes.back: As fabricated.

notes.front: In aluminium temper designations, what does the letter O after the alloy number mean?
notes.explanation: It is the soft condition of the metal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Hardness Identification”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: These designations are as follows: • F—as fabricated • O—annealed, recrystallized (wrought products only) • H—strain hardened
notes.back: Annealed, recrystallised (wrought products only).

notes.front: In aluminium temper designations, what does the letter H after the alloy number mean?
notes.explanation: Cold-working hardens the metal, and digits after the H give the degree of strain hardening.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Hardness Identification”, p. 7-7
notes.evidence: These designations are as follows: • F—as fabricated • O—annealed, recrystallized (wrought products only) • H—strain hardened
notes.back: Strain hardened.

notes.front: In aluminium temper designations, what does the letter W after the alloy number mean?
notes.explanation: The alloy keeps ageing naturally, so W is given only with the ageing period, for example 7075-W (½ hour).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: • W—solution heat-treated, unstable temper • T—treated to produce stable tempers other than F, O, or H
notes.back: Solution heat-treated, unstable temper.

notes.front: In aluminium temper designations, what does the letter T after the alloy number mean?
notes.explanation: Digits after the T, such as 3, 4 or 6, name the exact treatment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: • W—solution heat-treated, unstable temper • T—treated to produce stable tempers other than F, O, or H
notes.back: Treated to produce stable tempers other than F, O or H.

notes.front: A sheet is marked `2024-T3`. What treatment has it had?
notes.explanation: The temper follows the alloy number after a dash, and `T3` names solution heat-treatment followed by cold-working.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: • T2—annealed (cast products only) • T3—solution heat-treated and then cold-worked • T4—solution heat-treated
notes.back: A) Solution heat-treated and then cold-worked
notes.choices:
A) Solution heat-treated and then cold-worked
B) Solution heat-treated and then artificially aged
C) Annealed and recrystallised
D) Artificially aged only
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is `T6`. C: that is the O temper. D: that is `T5`.

notes.front: Why should clad aluminium be heated as quickly as possible and not held too long at heat-treating temperature?
notes.explanation: Excessive diffusion may defeat the purpose of cladding; for the same reason clad sheet is allowed only one to three reheat-treatments.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Time at Temperature”, p. 7-22
notes.evidence: With clad material, prolonged heating results in excessive diffusion of copper and other soluble constituents into the protective cladding and may defeat the purpose of cladding.
notes.back: Long heating lets copper and other constituents of the core diffuse into the cladding, reducing its corrosion resistance.

notes.front: An unmarked aluminium sheet is dipped in 10 percent caustic soda. The surface stays bright, but the edge shows a dark area in the middle. What is it?
notes.explanation: Heat-treatable alloys turn black because of their copper; on clad sheet only the core, seen at the edge, darkens.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: The heat-treatable alloys turn black due to the copper content, whereas the others remain bright. In the case of clad material, the surface remains bright, but there is a dark area in the middle when viewed from the edge.
notes.back: D) Clad sheet with a heat-treatable core
notes.choices:
A) A non-heat-treatable alloy with no cladding
B) Bare heat-treatable alloy
C) Commercially pure aluminium throughout
D) Clad sheet with a heat-treatable core
notes.choicesExplained: A: non-heat-treatable alloys stay bright right through, with no dark core at the edge. B: bare heat-treatable alloy turns black on the surface as well. C: pure aluminium has no copper to turn black, so no dark band would show.

notes.front: How should a magnesium fire be fought, and what must not be used?
notes.explanation: Water or foam makes magnesium burn more rapidly and can cause explosions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Magnesium & Magnesium Alloys”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: Should a fire occur, it could be extinguished with an extinguishing powder, such as soapstone or graphite. Water or any standard liquid or foam fire extinguisher causes magnesium to burn more rapidly and can cause explosions.
notes.back: With an extinguishing powder such as soapstone or graphite; never water or standard liquid or foam extinguishers.

notes.front: Fine magnesium chips under a drill press catch fire. What should the mechanic reach for?
notes.explanation: Soapstone or graphite powder is the handbook’s way to put out magnesium fires.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Magnesium & Magnesium Alloys”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: However, magnesium dust and fine chips are ignited easily. Precautions must be taken to avoid this if possible. Should a fire occur, it could be extinguished with an extinguishing powder, such as soapstone or graphite.
notes.back: D) A dry extinguishing powder such as graphite
notes.choices:
A) A water extinguisher
B) A foam extinguisher
C) Nothing, since magnesium will not burn below 1,204 °F
D) A dry extinguishing powder such as graphite
notes.choicesExplained: A: water makes magnesium burn more rapidly and can cause explosions. B: foam, like other standard liquid agents, makes the fire worse. C: that applies to large sections; dust and fine chips ignite easily.

notes.front: How does the weight of titanium compare with aluminium and stainless steel?
notes.explanation: Its ultimate yield strength drops rapidly above 800 °F, so its high melting point does not give good high-temperature properties.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Titanium and Titanium Alloys”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: Titanium is approximately 60 percent heavier than aluminum and about 50 percent lighter than stainless steel. Because of the high melting point of titanium, high temperature properties are disappointing. The ultimate yield strength of titanium drops rapidly above 800 °F.
notes.back: About 60 percent heavier than aluminium and about 50 percent lighter than stainless steel.

notes.front: A part looks like stainless steel but might be titanium. Which quick check does the handbook describe?
notes.explanation: Titanium resembles stainless steel, so the handbook gives the spark test (brilliant white burst) and the glass line.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Titanium and Titanium Alloys”, p. 7-9
notes.evidence: Titanium, in appearance, is like stainless steel. One quick method used to identify titanium is the spark test. Titanium gives off a brilliant white trace ending in a brilliant white burst. Also, moistening the titanium and using it to draw a line on a piece of glass can accomplish identification.
notes.back: D) Moisten it and draw a line on glass: titanium leaves a dark, pencil-like line
notes.choices:
A) Check it with a magnet, since titanium is magnetic
B) Look for a copper-coloured spot after cupric chloride
C) Dip it in caustic soda and look for black
D) Moisten it and draw a line on glass: titanium leaves a dark, pencil-like line
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook gives no copper-spot test; its spot test for Inconel against stainless steel shows pink or brown. C: that separates heat-treatable from non-heat-treatable aluminium. A: titanium is nonmagnetic.

notes.front: When substituting a metal in a repair, what is the first and most important requirement, and what are the other three?
notes.explanation: Strength comes first; the other three protect the aircraft’s shape, weight and resistance to corrosion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Substitution of Aircraft Metals”, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: The first and most important of these is maintaining the original strength of the structure. The other three are maintaining contour or aerodynamic smoothness; maintaining original weight, if possible, or keeping added weight to a minimum; and maintaining the original corrosionresistant properties of the metal.
notes.back: First, keep the original strength. Then keep contour or aerodynamic smoothness, original weight (or add little) and original corrosion resistance.

notes.front: A mechanic wants to replace a damaged rib with a different alloy that is available in stock. What should be checked first?
notes.explanation: Manufacturers design members for specific loads, so the structural repair manual is the starting point for any substitution.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Substitution of Aircraft Metals”, p. 7-11
notes.evidence: In selecting substitute metals for the repair and maintenance of aircraft, it is very important to check the appropriate structural repair manual. Aircraft manufacturers design structural members to meet a specific load requirement for an
notes.back: A) The appropriate structural repair manual
notes.choices:
A) The appropriate structural repair manual
B) Whichever alloy is lightest, since weight is the first requirement
C) Any alloy of the same thickness, since apparently similar members are repaired alike
D) The alloy with the best corrosion resistance
notes.choicesExplained: B: keeping original strength comes first, not weight. C: repair methods for similar-looking members vary with different aircraft. D: corrosion resistance is one of the four requirements, but not the first check or the first requirement.

notes.front: What does cold-working do to a metal’s strength, hardness, elastic limit and ductility?
notes.explanation: The metal becomes more brittle, so during some operations it must be heated from time to time to remove the undesirable effects.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cold-Working/Hardening”, p. 7-29
notes.evidence: The strength and hardness, as well as the elastic limit, are increased; but the ductility decreases. Since this makes the metal more brittle, it must be heated from time to time during certain operations to remove the undesirable effects of the working.
notes.back: Strength, hardness and elastic limit increase; ductility decreases.

notes.front: How does cold-working differ from hot-working in temperature and result?
notes.explanation: Almost all steel is hot-worked from the ingot first, and hot-rolled material is often finished by cold rolling or drawing for accurate dimensions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cold-Working/Hardening”, p. 7-29
notes.evidence: Cold-working applies to mechanical working performed at temperatures below the critical range. It results in a strain hardening of the metal.
notes.back: Cold-working is mechanical working below the critical range and strain hardens the metal; hot-working is done above that range.

notes.front: A mechanic bends a small aluminium tab back and forth at the same spot several times to adjust it. What does the handbook warn will happen?
notes.explanation: Practically all of a mechanic’s metalwork is cold-work, which hardens the metal; worked too much in one place, it cracks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cold-Working”, p. 7-13
notes.evidence: Practically all the work an aviation mechanic does on metal is cold-work. While this is convenient, it causes the metal to become harder and more
notes.back: B) The metal work-hardens and can crack or break
notes.choices:
A) The metal becomes softer and more ductile
B) The metal work-hardens and can crack or break
C) Nothing, because cold-work has no effect on aluminium
D) The metal anneals itself at room temperature
notes.choicesExplained: A: cold-work makes metal harder and more brittle, not softer. C: aluminium becomes stronger and harder as it is cold-worked. D: annealing needs heating to a prescribed temperature.

notes.front: Why is steel heated relatively slowly in heat-treatment, and at what furnace temperature is cold steel usually put in?
notes.explanation: Starting in a cooler furnace prevents too rapid heating through the critical range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heating”, p. 7-15
notes.evidence: this transition takes time, a relatively slow rate of heating must be used. Ordinarily, the cold steel is inserted when the temperature in the furnace is from 300 °F to 500 °F below the hardening temperature. In this way, too rapid heating through the critical range is prevented.
notes.back: Its change to austenite takes time; it goes in when the furnace is 300 °F to 500 °F below the hardening temperature.

notes.front: How long is a typical soaking period in steel heat-treatment, and which parts need longer?
notes.explanation: The length of the soak depends on the type of steel and the size of the part.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Soaking”, p. 7-16
notes.evidence: The length of the soaking period depends upon the type of steel and the size of the part. Naturally, heavier parts require longer soaking to ensure equal heating throughout. As a general rule, a soaking period of 30 minutes to 1 hour is sufficient for the average heat-treating operation.
notes.back: 30 minutes to 1 hour for the average operation; heavier parts need longer to heat equally throughout.

notes.front: In heat-treatment, what does the rate of cooling through the critical range decide?
notes.explanation: Different cooling rates give different results: still air is slow, and liquids are fastest, which is why liquids are used to harden steel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cooling”, p. 7-16
notes.evidence: The rate of cooling through the critical range determines the form that the steel retains. Various rates of cooling are used to produce the desired results. Still air is a slow cooling medium but is much faster than furnace cooling. Liquids are the fastest cooling media and are therefore used in hardening steels.
notes.back: The form the steel retains.

notes.front: Which of the three common quenching liquids is strongest and which weakest, and which suits alloy steels?
notes.explanation: Quenching media act only by cooling the steel; they have no beneficial chemical action on it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Quenching Media”, p. 7-16
notes.evidence: There are three commonly used quenching liquids: brine, water, and oil. Brine is the strongest quenching medium, water is next, and oil is the least. Generally, an oil quench is used for alloy steels and brine or water for carbon steels.
notes.back: Brine, then water, then oil; oil is generally used for alloy steels, brine or water for carbon steels.

notes.front: A heat-treater is about to drop an irregularly shaped hot steel part into the quench tank. What does the handbook recommend?
notes.explanation: Parts of an article cool at different rates, and these steps greatly reduce the tendency to warp.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Quenching”, p. 7-16
notes.evidence: 1. Never throw a part into the quenching bath. By permitting it to lie on the bottom of the bath, it is apt to cool faster on the topside than on the bottom side, thus causing it to warp or crack.
notes.back: D) Lower it heavy end first and agitate it slightly
notes.choices:
A) Throw it in and let it lie on the bottom
B) Hold it still so the vapour coat stays even
C) Lower it light end first so it cools slowly
D) Lower it heavy end first and agitate it slightly
notes.choicesExplained: A: a part lying on the bottom cools faster on top than underneath and may warp or crack. B: the vapour coating should be broken up by slight agitation. C: the recommendation is for the heavy end to enter first.

notes.front: What does the hardening treatment for most steels consist of?
notes.explanation: Oil, water or brine give the rapid cooling that hardening needs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Hardening”, p. 7-17
notes.evidence: For most steels, the hardening treatment consists of heating the steel to a temperature just above the upper critical point, soaking or holding for the required length of time, and then cooling it rapidly by plunging the hot steel into oil, water, or brine.
notes.back: Heating just above the upper critical point, soaking for the required time, then cooling rapidly in oil, water or brine.

notes.front: A carbon steel part has been quenched for hardening. When should it come out of the bath, and what happens next?
notes.explanation: As-quenched steel has high internal stresses, and 200 °F down to room temperature is the cracking range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Hardening”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Because of the high internal stresses in the “as quenched” condition, steel must be tempered just before it becomes cold. The part should be removed from the quenching bath at a temperature of approximately 200 °F, since the temperature range from 200 °F down to room temperature is the cracking range.
notes.back: B) At about 200 °F, then it is tempered before it becomes cold
notes.choices:
A) At room temperature, then it is used as quenched
B) At about 200 °F, then it is tempered before it becomes cold
C) At about 1,000 °F, then it is air cooled
D) At about 200 °F, then it is annealed
notes.choicesExplained: A: 200 °F down to room temperature is the cracking range, and as-quenched steel has high internal stresses. C: carbon steel must drop below 1,000 °F within 1 second and keep cooling to become martensite. D: annealing would soften it again; tempering is what follows hardening.

notes.front: At what temperature does tempering of hardened steel begin?
notes.explanation: Choosing a definite tempering temperature predetermines the resulting hardness and strength.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Tempering”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: When hardened steel is reheated, tempering begins at 212 °F and continues as the temperature increases toward the low critical point. By selecting a definite tempering temperature, the resulting hardness and strength can be predetermined.
notes.back: 212 °F, continuing as the temperature rises toward the low critical point.

notes.front: A steel fitting 3 inches thick is to be tempered. What is the minimum time at the tempering temperature?
notes.explanation: The minimum is 1 hour, plus 1 hour for each additional inch over one inch: 1 + 2 = 3.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Tempering”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: The minimum time at the tempering temperature should be 1 hour. If the part is over one inch in thickness, increase the time by 1 hour for each additional inch of thickness.
notes.back: A) 3 hours
notes.choices:
A) 3 hours
B) 1 hour
C) 30 minutes
D) 6 hours
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the minimum only for parts up to one inch thick. C: that is a typical soaking time for hardening, not tempering. D: the rule adds 1 hour per additional inch, not 2.

notes.front: When steel is annealed for maximum softness, how long is it soaked and how is it cooled?
notes.explanation: Maximum softness in steel needs very slow cooling.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Annealing”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: Soaking time is approximately 1 hour per inch of thickness of the material. To produce maximum softness in steel, the metal must be cooled very slowly. Slow cooling is obtained by shutting off the heat and allowing the furnace and metal to cool together to 900 °F or lower
notes.back: About 1 hour per inch of thickness; then cooled with the furnace to 900 °F or lower before finishing in still air.

notes.front: An aluminium part has become too hard to finish forming after a long forming operation. What does the handbook suggest?
notes.explanation: Annealing leaves aluminium in the best condition for cold-working, and prolonged forming causes “mechanical hardness”.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Annealing of Aluminum Alloys”, p. 7-23
notes.evidence: Annealing leaves the metal in the best condition for cold-working. However, when prolonged forming operations are involved, the metal takes on a condition known as “mechanical hardness” and resists further working. It may be necessary to anneal a part several times during the forming process to avoid cracking.
notes.back: C) Anneal it, possibly several times during forming, to avoid cracking
notes.choices:
A) Keep forming it cold until it shapes
B) Temper it
C) Anneal it, possibly several times during forming, to avoid cracking
D) Normalise it
notes.choicesExplained: A: the metal resists further working and may crack. B: tempering is a steel process; no nonferrous metal can be tempered. D: normalising applies to iron-base metals only.

notes.front: Why should welded steel parts be normalised after fabrication?
notes.explanation: Welding strains the adjacent material, and the weld is a cast structure with a different grain size from the wrought metal around it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Normalizing”, p. 7-19
notes.evidence: These two types of structures have different grain sizes, and to refine the grain as well as to relieve the internal stresses, all welded parts should be normalized after fabrication.
notes.back: To refine the grain and relieve internal stresses.

notes.front: Which of these metals can be normalised?
notes.explanation: Normalising applies to iron-base metals only, and welded steel parts are prime candidates.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Normalizing”, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: Normalizing applies to iron base metals only. Normalizing consists of heating the part to the proper temperature, holding it at that temperature until it is uniformly heated, and then cooling it in still air.
notes.back: B) A welded chrome-molybdenum steel tube
notes.choices:
A) A 2024 aluminium fitting
B) A welded chrome-molybdenum steel tube
C) A magnesium casting
D) A titanium firewall
notes.choicesExplained: A: normalising applies to iron-base metals only. D: no nonferrous metal can be normalised. C: magnesium is nonferrous, and normalising applies to iron-base metals only.

notes.front: How does nitriding differ from other case hardening processes?
notes.explanation: The nitriding itself is then done at about 1,000 °F in ammonia gas.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Nitriding”, p. 7-20
notes.evidence: Nitriding is unlike other case hardening processes in that, before nitriding, the part is heat-treated to produce definite physical properties. Thus, parts are hardened and tempered before being nitrided.
notes.back: Before nitriding, the part is already heat-treated, hardened and tempered, to definite physical properties.

notes.front: A low-carbon steel part needs a wear-resistant surface but a tough interior. Which treatment packs it in charcoal in a sealed container at about 1,700 °F?
notes.explanation: Carburising adds carbon to the surface of low-carbon steel, giving a high-carbon case over a low-carbon core.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Carburizing”, p. 7-20
notes.evidence: When carburizing is to be done by this method, the steel parts are packed in a container with charcoal or some other material rich in carbon. The container is then sealed with fire clay, placed in a furnace, heated to approximately 1,700 °F,
notes.back: B) Pack carburising
notes.choices:
A) Nitriding
B) Pack carburising
C) Cyaniding
