D) Normalising
notes.choicesExplained: A: nitriding uses ammonia gas at about 1,000 °F. C: cyaniding is not used in aircraft work. D: normalising relieves stresses; it does not make a hard case.

notes.front: Within what range are solution heat-treating temperatures for aluminium alloys, and how closely must they be held?
notes.explanation: If the temperature is too low, maximum strength is not obtained.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Solution Heat-Treatment Temperature”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: The temperatures used for solution heat-treating vary with different alloys and range from 825 °F to 980 °F. As a rule, they must be controlled within a very narrow range (±10 °F) to obtain specified properties. If the temperature is too low, maximum strength is not obtained.
notes.back: 825 °F to 980 °F, depending on the alloy, controlled within ±10 °F.

notes.front: Which alloys develop full properties from solution heat-treatment plus about 4 days of room-temperature ageing, and which need both heat-treatments?
notes.explanation: Alloys needing artificial ageing still age a little at room temperature, by an amount that depends on the alloy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: Some alloys, such as 2017 and 2024, develop their full properties as a result of solution heat-treatment followed by about 4 days of aging at room temperature. Other alloys, such as 2014 and 7075, require both heat-treatments.
notes.back: 2017 and 2024 age naturally; 2014 and 7075 need solution and precipitation heat-treatment.

notes.front: Before quenching a batch of 2024 sheet after solution heat-treatment, the quench water reads 95 °F. What should be done?
notes.explanation: Sheet, extrusions, tubing and small forgings are quenched in cold water no warmer than 85 °F.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cold Water Quenching”, p. 7-22
notes.evidence: Parts produced from sheet, extrusions, tubing, small forgings, and similar type material are generally quenched in a cold water bath. The temperature of the water before quenching should not exceed 85 °F.
notes.back: A) Cool the water to 85 °F or below before quenching
notes.choices:
A) Cool the water to 85 °F or below before quenching
B) Quench anyway; any water temperature gives the same result
C) Switch to a hot water quench
D) Let the sheet cool in air for a minute first
notes.choicesExplained: B: the water must not exceed 85 °F, and a drastic quench gives maximum corrosion resistance. C: hot water is for large forgings and heavy sections, not sheet. D: 2017 and 2024 sheet must reach the quench within 10 seconds.

notes.front: What is the longest allowed time between leaving the furnace and quenching when solution heat-treating 2017 or 2024 sheet?
notes.explanation: Cooling before the quench promotes re-precipitation along grain boundaries, which causes poorer formability.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Lag Between Soaking & Quenching”, p. 7-22
notes.evidence: The elapsed time must not exceed 10 seconds when solution heat-treating 2017 or 2024 sheet material. The allowable time for heavy sections may be slightly greater. Allowing the metal to cool slightly before quenching promotes re-precipitation from the solid solution. The precipitation occurs along grain boundaries and in certain slip planes causing poorer formability.
notes.back: 10 seconds.

notes.front: What temperatures are used for precipitation-hardening aluminium alloys, and how closely are they held?
notes.explanation: Holding the temperature this tightly is what the handbook says gives the best results.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Precipitation Practices”, p. 7-23
notes.evidence: The temperatures used for precipitation-hardening depend upon the alloy and the properties desired, ranging from 250 °F to 375 °F. They should be controlled within a very narrow range (±5 °F)
notes.back: 250 °F to 375 °F, depending on alloy and properties wanted, within ±5 °F.

notes.front: After precipitation treatment, a technician leaves the parts to cool slowly inside the furnace. What does the handbook warn this tends to cause?
notes.explanation: After the thermal precipitation treatment the material should be air cooled, since furnace cooling tends to over-age it and strength declines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Precipitation Practices”, p. 7-23
notes.evidence: After receiving the thermal precipitation treatment, the material should be air cooled to room temperature. Water quenching, while not necessary, produces no ill effects. Furnace cooling tends to produce over-aging.
notes.back: D) Over-ageing
notes.choices:
A) Too little ageing
B) Quench cracking
C) Nothing; furnace cooling is the recommended practice
D) Over-ageing
notes.choicesExplained: A: slow furnace cooling prolongs the heat, which over-ages rather than under-ages. B: cracking comes from unequal temperatures in a quench, not from furnace cooling. C: the recommendation is to air cool to room temperature.

notes.front: Kept in a refrigerator below 32 °F, how long do icebox rivets stay soft enough to drive?
notes.explanation: Both passages give below 32 °F; because the two figures differ, expect either in questions, and reheat-treat rivets not used in time.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Solid Shank Rivets”, p. 7-52
notes.evidence: They are referred to as “icebox” rivets. Under this storage condition, they remain soft enough for driving for up to 2 weeks. Any rivets not used within that time should be removed for reheat-treating.
notes.back: Up to 2 weeks, says the handbook’s rivet section; its heat-treatment section says only “several days”.

notes.front: Once out of refrigeration, how soon must 2017-T and 2024-T rivets be driven?
notes.explanation: The rivet section is stricter: 2017-T out for 1 hour or more, or 2024-T out for over 10 minutes, must be reheat-treated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Aluminum Alloy Rivets”, p. 7-24
notes.evidence: The 2017 rivet should be driven within approximately 1 hour and the 2024 rivet within 10 to 20 minutes after heat-treating or removal from refrigeration. If not used within these times, the rivets should be reheat-treated before being refrigerated.
notes.back: 2017-T within about 1 hour; 2024-T within 10 to 20 minutes.

notes.front: A mechanic takes out more 2024-T icebox rivets than can be driven in 15 minutes. What should happen to the extras?
notes.explanation: Icebox rivets taken out must not be mixed with cold ones, and any not usable in 15 minutes go aside for reheat-treatment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Icebox Rivets”, p. 7-54
notes.evidence: Once an icebox rivet has been taken from the refrigerator, it should not be mixed with the rivets still in cold storage. If more rivets are removed from the refrigerator than can be used in 15 minutes, they should be placed in a separate container and stored for reheat-treatment.
notes.back: C) Put them in a separate container for reheat-treatment
notes.choices:
A) Return them to the refrigerator with the others
B) Drive them later the same day
C) Put them in a separate container for reheat-treatment
D) Use them as field rivets
notes.choicesExplained: A: once out, icebox rivets should not be mixed with those still in cold storage. B: 2024-T rivets exposed for more than 10 minutes must be reheat-treated. D: field rivets are 2117-T, a different alloy that needs no heat-treatment.

notes.front: In non-heat-treatable aluminium alloys, what gives the mechanical properties, and what destroys them?
notes.explanation: Heat undoes what cold-work gave these alloys, so only more cold-work can restore the properties.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wrought Aluminum”, p. 7-6
notes.evidence: Non-heat-treatable alloys are those in which the mechanical properties are determined by the amount of cold-work introduced after the final annealing operation. The mechanical properties obtained by cold-working are destroyed by any subsequent heating and cannot be restored except by additional cold-working, which is not always possible.
notes.back: Cold-work after the final anneal gives them; any later heating destroys them.

notes.front: An unmarked, unclad aluminium sample turns black in 10 percent caustic soda. What does that show?
notes.explanation: Heat-treatable alloys turn black because of their copper content, while the others stay bright.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Heat-Treatment of Nonferrous Metals”, p. 7-21
notes.evidence: it is possible to separate the heat-treatable alloys from the nonheat-treatable alloys by immersing a sample of the material in a 10 percent solution of caustic soda (sodium hydroxide). The heat-treatable alloys turn black due to the copper content, whereas the others remain bright.
notes.back: A) It is a heat-treatable alloy
notes.choices:
A) It is a heat-treatable alloy
B) It is a non-heat-treatable alloy
C) It is clad sheet
D) It is magnesium
notes.choicesExplained: B: non-heat-treatable alloys remain bright. C: clad sheet stays bright on the surface with a dark core at the edge. D: the test separates heat-treatable from non-heat-treatable aluminium alloys.

notes.front: What penetrator does the Brinell hardness tester use?
notes.explanation: The load differs by metal: 3,000 kilograms for ferrous metals and 500 for nonferrous.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Brinell Tester”, p. 7-26
notes.evidence: The Brinell hardness tester uses a hardened spherical ball that is forced into the surface of the metal. [Figure 7-9] This ball is 10 millimeters (0.3937 inch) in diameter. A pressure of 3,000 kilograms is used for ferrous metals and 500 kilograms for nonferrous metals.
notes.back: A hardened steel ball 10 millimetres in diameter, forced into the metal’s surface.

notes.front: What Rockwell tester set-up is used for hardened steels?
notes.explanation: The reading is recorded with the letter C in front of the number.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Rockwell Tester”, p. 7-26
notes.evidence: For hardened steels, the diamond penetrator is used; the major load is 150 kilograms; and the hardness is read on the “C” scale. When this reading is recorded, the letter “C” must precede the number indicated by the pointer.
notes.back: A diamond penetrator, a 150-kilogram major load, and the “C” scale.

notes.front: What is the Barcol tester for, and where must it not be used?
notes.explanation: Its range is roughly 25 to 100 Brinell, which covers the softer metals it is designed for.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Barcol Tester”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: The Barcol tester is a portable unit designed for testing aluminum alloys, copper, brass, or other relatively soft materials. [Figure 7-12] It should not be used on aircraft steels. Approximate range of the tester is 25 to 100 Brinell.
notes.back: A portable tester for aluminium alloys, copper, brass and other relatively soft materials; not for aircraft steels.

notes.front: An inspector wants to confirm the heat-treatment of an aluminium fitting that is already installed in the aircraft. Which tester suits the job?
notes.explanation: The portable Barcol tester works in any position and is of great value on assembled or installed parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Barcol Tester”, p. 7-27
notes.evidence: The unit can be used in any position and in any space that allows for the operator’s hand. It is of great value in the hardness testing of assembled or installed parts, especially to check for proper heat-treatment.
notes.back: B) The Barcol tester
notes.choices:
A) The Brinell tester
B) The Barcol tester
C) The Rockwell tester with the diamond penetrator
D) A spark test
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is a bench machine with anvils and a hydraulic pump, not a hand-held tool for installed parts. C: the specimen must be ground smooth and locked on an anvil, and the diamond set-up is for hard steels. D: spark testing identifies ferrous metals; it does not measure hardness.

notes.front: What are two advantages of composites the handbook lists?
notes.explanation: The list also includes longer life than metals and fibre-to-fibre stress transfer through chemical bonding.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Advantages/Disadvantages of Composites”, p. 7-30
notes.evidence: Some of the many advantages for using composite materials are: • High strength-to-weight ratio • Fiber-to-fiber transfer of stress allowed by chemical bonding • Modulus (stiffness-to-density ratio) 3.5 to 5 times that of steel or aluminum • Longer life than metals • Higher corrosion resistance • Tensile strength 4 to 6 times that of steel or aluminum
notes.back: Any two, for example: high strength-to-weight ratio, tensile strength 4 to 6 times that of steel or aluminium, and higher corrosion resistance.

notes.front: An inspector is asked which difficulty the handbook lists first among composite disadvantages. What is it?
notes.explanation: The handbook notes technology will eventually correct the inspection problem, but lists it first.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Advantages/Disadvantages of Composites”, p. 7-30
notes.evidence: The disadvantages of composites include: • Inspection methods difficult to conduct, especially delamination detection (Advancements in technology will eventually correct this problem.)
notes.back: A) Inspection is difficult, especially detecting delamination
notes.choices:
A) Inspection is difficult, especially detecting delamination
B) Low strength-to-weight ratio
C) Low corrosion resistance
D) Joints and fasteners are needed everywhere
notes.choicesExplained: C: higher corrosion resistance is listed as an advantage. B: high strength-to-weight ratio is an advantage. D: bonded construction eliminating joints and fasteners is an advantage.

notes.front: A technician is about to sand and apply resin to a fibreglass repair. Which eye protection does the handbook call for?
notes.explanation: Chemical damage to the eyes is usually irreversible, so goggles without vent holes are required with resins or solvents.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Composite Safety”, p. 7-31
notes.evidence: The eyes must be protected using leak-proof goggles (no vent holes) when working with resins or solvents, because chemical damage to the eyes is usually irreversible.
notes.back: C) Leak-proof goggles with no vent holes
notes.choices:
A) Ordinary safety glasses
B) Vented goggles for comfort
C) Leak-proof goggles with no vent holes
D) None if a dust mask is worn
notes.choicesExplained: A: resins and solvents call for leak-proof goggles, since chemical eye damage is usually irreversible. B: the goggles must have no vent holes. D: a dust mask protects the lungs, not the eyes.

notes.front: Which synthetic rubber does the handbook give for use with phosphate ester hydraulic fluids?
notes.explanation: Like natural rubber, though, butyl swells in petroleum or coal tar solvents.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Synthetic Rubber”, p. 7-32
notes.evidence: Like natural rubber, butyl swells in petroleum or coal tar solvents. It has a low water absorption rate and good resistance to heat and low temperature. Depending on the grade, it is suitable for use in temperatures ranging from −65 °F to 300 °F. Butyl is used with phosphate ester hydraulic fluids (Skydrol™), silicone fluids, gases, ketones, and acetones.
notes.back: Butyl.

notes.front: Above what pressure are backup rings used with O-rings, and how many are used with pressure from both sides?
notes.explanation: Backup rings prevent the O-ring from extruding.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “O-Ring Packings”, p. 7-34
notes.evidence: In installations subject to pressures above 1,500 psi, backup rings are used with O-rings to prevent extrusion. When O-ring packing is subjected to pressure from both sides, as in actuating cylinders, two backup rings must be used (one on either side of the O-ring).
notes.back: Above 1,500 psi; with pressure from both sides, two, one either side of the O-ring.

notes.front: On O-rings compatible with hydrocarbon fluid, the colour code always contains red but never contains {{c1::blue}}.
notes.explanation: Red is the constant element of the code for hydrocarbon-compatible rings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “O-Ring Packings”, p. 7-34
notes.evidence: Color codes on O-rings that are compatible with hydrocarbon fluid always contains red but never contain blue.

notes.front: A hydraulic O-ring bin has lost its labels, though some rings carry colour dots. What is the most reliable way to identify the right compound?
notes.explanation: Colour codes may be omitted or not permanent and give no age or temperature limit, so the envelope’s part number is the reliable guide.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “O-Ring Packings”, p. 7-34
notes.evidence: When selecting an O-ring for installation, the basic part number on the sealed envelope provides the most reliable compound
notes.back: C) The basic part number on the sealed envelope
notes.choices:
A) Size and texture by eye
B) The colour code on the ring
C) The basic part number on the sealed envelope
D) A stripe colour of red for hydraulic fluid
notes.choicesExplained: B: colour coding is not a reliable or complete means of identification. A: O-rings look alike but their characteristics may differ widely. D: a red stripe means fuel; blue means hydraulic fluid.

notes.front: Among the three classes of seals, what are packings used as?
notes.explanation: They are made of synthetic or natural rubber as O-rings, V-rings and U-rings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Packings”, p. 7-34
notes.evidence: Packings are made of synthetic or natural rubber. They are generally used as “running seals,” that is, in units that contain moving parts, such as actuating cylinders, pumps, selector valves, and so forth.
notes.back: Running seals in units with moving parts, such as actuating cylinders, pumps and selector valves.

notes.front: Among the three classes of seals, what are gaskets used as?
notes.explanation: Common materials include copper, cork and rubber.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Gaskets”, p. 7-35
notes.evidence: Gaskets are used as static (stationary) seals between two flat surfaces. Some of the more common gasket materials are asbestos, copper, cork, and rubber.
notes.back: Static seals between two flat surfaces.

notes.front: Among the three classes of seals, what are wipers used as?
notes.explanation: They help protect the shaft against scoring and may be metallic or felt.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Wipers”, p. 7-35
notes.evidence: Wipers are used to clean and lubricate the exposed portions of piston shafts. They prevent dirt from entering the system and help protect the piston shaft against scoring.
notes.back: Seals that clean and lubricate the exposed parts of piston shafts, keeping dirt out.

notes.front: A mechanic must seal the joint between a cast housing cover and its flat mating face, with no moving parts. Which class of seal fits?
notes.explanation: Gaskets are the static seals between two flat surfaces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Gaskets”, p. 7-35
notes.evidence: Gaskets are used as static (stationary) seals between two flat surfaces.
notes.back: B) A gasket
notes.choices:
A) A packing
B) A gasket
C) A wiper
D) A V-ring
notes.choicesExplained: A: packings are running seals for units with moving parts. C: wipers clean exposed piston shafts. D: a V-ring is a one-way packing for moving parts.

notes.front: What is the ideal curing condition for most sealants, and what temperature must never be exceeded?
notes.explanation: Curing can be sped up with heat, but it is extremely slow below 60 °F and must stay under the limit.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Two Part Sealants”, p. 7-36
notes.evidence: A temperature of 77 °F with 50 percent relative humidity is the ideal condition for curing most sealants. Curing may be accelerated by increasing the temperature, but the temperature should never be allowed to exceed 120 °F at any time in the curing cycle.
notes.back: 77 °F with 50 percent relative humidity; never above 120 °F in the curing cycle.

notes.front: Which class of thread fit are aircraft bolts almost always made in, and which do aircraft screws generally use?
notes.explanation: The class of a thread is the manufacturing tolerance; Class 4 needs a wrench to run the nut on, Class 1 turns easily by hand.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Classification of Threads”, p. 7-37
notes.evidence: Aircraft bolts are almost always manufactured in the Class 3, medium fit. A Class 4 fit requires a wrench to turn the nut onto a bolt, whereas a Class 1 fit can easily be turned by hand. Generally, aircraft screws are manufactured with a Class 2 thread fit for ease of assembly.
notes.back: Bolts: Class 3, medium fit. Screws: Class 2, free fit, for ease of assembly.

notes.front: A 1-inch bolt is described as American National Fine, and its replacement as American Standard Unified Fine. How many threads per inch does each have?
notes.explanation: The handbook points out this one difference between the American National and American Standard Unified series at the 1-inch size.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Classification of Threads”, p. 7-37
notes.evidence: In the 1-inch diameter size, the NF thread specifies 14 threads per inch (1-14 NF), while the UNF thread specifies 12 threads per inch (1-12 UNF).
notes.back: C) 14 for the American National Fine, 12 for the Unified Fine
notes.choices:
A) 12 for both
B) 14 for both
C) 14 for the American National Fine, 12 for the Unified Fine
D) 12 for the American National Fine, 14 for the Unified Fine
notes.choicesExplained: A: the two series differ at the 1-inch size. B: the Unified Fine thread has 12 per inch at this size. D: this reverses the two series.

notes.front: Which small bolts are not used in primary structures?
notes.explanation: Aluminium-alloy bolts and nuts are also kept out of places where they are removed repeatedly for maintenance and inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “General Purpose Bolts”, p. 7-38
notes.evidence: Alloy-steel bolts smaller than No. 10-32 and aluminumalloy bolts smaller than 1⁄4 inch in diameter are not used in primary structures. Aluminum-alloy bolts and nuts are not used where they are repeatedly removed for purposes of maintenance and inspection.
notes.back: Alloy-steel bolts smaller than No. 10-32 and aluminium-alloy bolts smaller than 1/4 inch in diameter.

notes.front: A mechanic plans to fit aluminium-alloy nuts on cadmium-plated steel shear bolts on a seaplane float fitting. Is this acceptable?
notes.explanation: Seaplanes have an increased possibility of dissimilar metal corrosion, so aluminium nuts are kept off them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “General Purpose Bolts”, p. 7-38
notes.evidence: Aluminum-alloy nuts may be used with cadmium-plated steel bolts loaded in shear on land airplanes, but are not used on seaplanes due to the increased possibility of dissimilar metal corrosion.
notes.back: C) No; they may be used on land aeroplanes but not on seaplanes
notes.choices:
A) Yes, on any aircraft, since the bolts are in shear
B) Yes, if the nuts are torqued to the high side of the range
C) No; they may be used on land aeroplanes but not on seaplanes
D) No, because aluminium nuts may never be used with steel bolts
notes.choicesExplained: A: the shear-load allowance applies to land aeroplanes only. B: torque does not address the dissimilar metal corrosion risk. D: they may be used with cadmium-plated steel shear bolts on land aeroplanes.

notes.front: How are close tolerance bolts of the National Aircraft Standard marked on the head?
notes.explanation: Their material markings otherwise match those on AN bolts, except that they may be raised or recessed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification and Coding”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: Close tolerance NAS bolts are marked with either a raised or recessed triangle. The material markings for NAS bolts are the same as for AN bolts, except that they may be either raised or recessed.
notes.back: With a raised or recessed triangle.

notes.front: A bolt slides into its reamed hole only when struck with a 12- to 14-ounce hammer. What kind of fit is this, and which bolt is it meant for?
notes.explanation: Fits are defined by the friction between bolt and hole, and close tolerance bolts are used where a tight drive fit is required.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Bolt & Hole Sizes”, p. 7-48
notes.evidence: A tight drive fit, for example, is one in which a sharp blow of a 12- or 14-ounce hammer is required to move the bolt. A bolt that requires a hard blow and sounds tight is considered too tight a fit.
notes.back: A) A tight drive fit, for a close tolerance bolt
notes.choices:
A) A tight drive fit, for a close tolerance bolt
B) A light drive fit, for a general purpose bolt
C) Too tight, so the hole must be reamed out
D) A clearance fit, for a tension-only bolt
notes.choicesExplained: B: a light-drive fit moves the bolt with a hammer handle pressed by body weight, not a hammer blow. C: too tight is a hard blow that sounds tight; a sharp 12- to 14-ounce blow is the tight drive fit. D: a clearance fit needs no hammer at all.

notes.front: On an aircraft bolt head, what do an asterisk, a triangle and the letter “S” each identify?
notes.explanation: Head markings generally show the maker, the material and whether a bolt is standard or special purpose.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification and Coding”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: dash or asterisk or a single raised dash.
notes.back: An asterisk (or raised dash): AN standard steel bolt. A triangle: close tolerance bolt. The letter “S”: special bolt.

image.alt: Three hexagonal bolt heads seen from above. The first carries an asterisk and is labelled AN standard steel bolt. The second carries a triangle and is labelled close tolerance bolt. The third carries the letter S and is labelled special bolt.

notes.front: In an AN bolt part number such as AN3DD5A, what does the 3 give?
notes.explanation: A matching nut’s dash number corresponds to this first figure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification and Coding”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: • The “3” indicates the diameter in sixteenths of an inch (3⁄16). • The “DD” indicates the material is 2024 aluminum alloy.
notes.back: The diameter in sixteenths of an inch: 3/16 inch.

notes.front: In an AN bolt part number such as AN3DD5A, what does the 5 give?
notes.explanation: The length figure follows the material letters in the part number.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification and Coding”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: • The “5” indicates the length in eighths of an inch (5⁄8).
notes.back: The length in eighths of an inch: 5/8 inch.

notes.front: In an AN bolt part number, what do the letters `DD`, C, or no letter after the diameter mean?
notes.explanation: The material letters sit between the diameter and length figures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification and Coding”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: • The “DD” indicates the material is 2024 aluminum alloy. • The letter “C” in place of the “DD” would indicate corrosion-resistant steel, and the absence of the letters would indicate cadmium-plated steel.
notes.back: `DD`: 2024 aluminium alloy. C: corrosion-resistant steel. No letter: cadmium-plated steel.

notes.front: A parts list calls for an AN bolt coded with an H before the length figure and an A after it. What does that tell the mechanic?
notes.explanation: The final A marks an undrilled shank, and an H before the length figure means the head is drilled.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification and Coding”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: the “A” indicates that the shank is undrilled. If the letter “H” preceded the “5” in addition to the “A” following it, the head would be drilled for safetying.
notes.back: B) The head is drilled for safetying and the shank is undrilled
notes.choices:
A) The shank is drilled and the head is undrilled
B) The head is drilled for safetying and the shank is undrilled
C) It is an aluminium-alloy bolt with a hex head
D) It is a high-strength internal wrenching bolt
notes.choicesExplained: A: A means the shank is undrilled, and H before the length means a drilled head. C: material is shown by letters such as `DD`, not by H or A. D: internal wrenching bolts carry different standard numbers.

notes.front: What loads is a clevis bolt used for?
notes.explanation: It is often inserted as a mechanical pin in a control system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Clevis Bolts”, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: This type of bolt is used only where shear loads occur and never in tension. It is often inserted as a mechanical pin in a control system.
notes.back: Shear loads only, never tension.

notes.front: Which non-self-locking nut, `AN310`, is used with drilled-shank bolts and slotted for a cotter pin or lock wire?
notes.explanation: It is rugged and withstands large tensional loads; its slots are called castellations.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Non-Self-Locking Nuts”, p. 7-42
notes.evidence: The castle nut, AN310, is used with drilled shank AN hex head bolts, Clevis bolts, eyebolts, drilled head bolts, or studs. It is rugged and can withstand large tensional loads. Slots (called castellations) in the nut are designed to accommodate a cotter pin or lock wire for safety.
notes.back: The castle nut.

notes.front: Which non-self-locking nut, `AN320`, is meant for devices under shearing stress only, such as drilled clevis bolts?
notes.explanation: It is not as deep or as strong as the castle nut, and its castellations are shallower.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Non-Self-Locking Nuts”, p. 7-42
notes.evidence: The castellated shear nut, AN320, is designed for use with devices, such as drilled Clevis bolts and threaded taper pins, which are normally subjected to shearing stress only.
notes.back: The castellated shear nut.

notes.front: Which non-self-locking nut, `AN350`, is used where hand tightness is enough and the assembly is often removed?
notes.explanation: It needs no wrench, which suits frequently removed assemblies.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Non-Self-Locking Nuts”, p. 7-42
notes.evidence: The wing nut, AN350, is intended for use where the desired tightness can be obtained by hand and where the assembly is frequently removed.
notes.back: The wing nut.

notes.front: A mechanic is fitting a nut on a drilled clevis bolt that carries shear only in a control linkage, to be safetied with a cotter pin. Which nut suits it?
notes.explanation: The castellated shear nut is designed for drilled clevis bolts under shearing stress and is castellated for safetying.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Non-Self-Locking Nuts”, p. 7-42
notes.evidence: The castellated shear nut, AN320, is designed for use with devices, such as drilled Clevis bolts and threaded taper pins, which are normally subjected to shearing stress only. Like the castle nut, it is castellated for safetying.
notes.back: D) A castellated shear nut
notes.choices:
A) A plain hex nut
B) A wing nut
C) A light hex nut
D) A castellated shear nut
notes.choicesExplained: A: it needs an auxiliary locking device such as a check nut or lock washer and has no slots for a cotter pin. B: wing nuts are for hand-tightened, frequently removed assemblies. C: it is for light tension requirements and must be locked by an auxiliary device.

notes.front: What are the two general types of self-locking nut?
notes.explanation: The handbook takes the Boots and stainless steel nuts as all-metal examples, and the elastic stop nut for the fibre insert type.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Self-Locking Nuts”, p. 7-43
notes.evidence: The two general types of self-locking nuts currently in use are the all-metal type and the fiber lock type. For the sake of simplicity, only three typical kinds of self-locking nuts are considered in this handbook: the Boots self-locking and the stainless steel self-locking nuts, representing the all-metal types; and the elastic stop nut, representing the fiber insert type.
notes.back: The all-metal type and the fibre lock (nonmetallic insert) type.

notes.front: Above what temperature must elastic stop nuts not be installed, and when should a used one be replaced?
notes.explanation: Beyond 250 °F the self-locking action is less effective, and a finger-turnable nut has lost its locking friction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Elastic Stop Nut”, p. 7-45
notes.evidence: Do not install elastic stop nuts in places where the temperature is higher than 250 °F, because the effectiveness of the selflocking action is reduced beyond this point.
notes.back: Not above 250 °F; replace one that can be turned with the fingers.

notes.front: A mechanic removes an elastic stop nut and finds it spins freely on the bolt using only fingers. What should be done?
notes.explanation: Before reuse, the fibre must not have lost its locking friction or become brittle; a nut turnable by hand has.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Elastic Stop Nut”, p. 7-44
notes.evidence: When reusing elastic stop nuts, be sure the fiber has not lost its locking friction or become brittle. If a nut can be turned with the fingers, replace it.
notes.back: C) Replace it
notes.choices:
A) Reuse it, since elastic stop nuts can be used many times
B) Tap a new thread into the fibre collar
C) Replace it
D) Reuse it with a lock washer underneath
notes.choicesExplained: A: reuse is allowed only while the fibre keeps its locking friction. B: the fibre insert must never be tapped. D: the nut’s own locking has failed; a lock washer does not restore it.

notes.front: According to Advisory Circular 43.13-1B, on what parts must self-locking nuts not be used?
notes.explanation: Self-locking castellated nuts with cotter pins or lock wire, however, may be used in any system.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-64, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: a. DO NOT use self-locking nuts on parts subject to rotation. b. Self-locking castellated nuts with cotter pins or lock wire may be used in any system.
notes.back: Parts subject to rotation.

notes.front: Where on turbine-engine aeroplanes should self-locking nuts not be used?
notes.explanation: The advisory circular also keeps them off access panels or doors that are routinely removed before or after each flight.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-64, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: c. Self-locking nuts should not be used with bolts or screws on turbine engine airplanes in locations where the loose nut, bolt, washer, or screw could fall or be drawn into the engine air intake scoop.
notes.back: Where a loose nut, bolt, washer or screw could fall or be drawn into the engine air intake scoop.

notes.front: An access panel is opened before every flight. A mechanic proposes self-locking nuts for its bolts. What does the advisory circular say?
notes.explanation: Repeated removal and installation makes self-locking nuts lose their locking feature.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-64, p. 7-12
notes.evidence: d. Self-locking nuts should not be used with bolts, screws, or studs to attach access panels or doors, or to assemble any parts that are routinely disassembled before or after each flight.
notes.back: B) They should not be used for parts routinely disassembled before or after each flight
notes.choices:
A) They are ideal, because they need no safety wire
B) They should not be used for parts routinely disassembled before or after each flight
C) They may be used if they are the fibre type
D) They may be used if torqued to the high side
notes.choicesExplained: A: the circular specifically excludes routinely removed panels and doors. C: the restriction covers both the all-metal and fibre types. D: torque does not change the restriction.

notes.front: What do plain washers do in a bolt and nut assembly?
notes.explanation: They also go under lock washers to protect the surface material.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Plain Washers”, p. 7-46
notes.evidence: They provide a smooth bearing surface and act as a shim in obtaining correct grip length for a bolt and nut assembly. They are used to adjust the position of castellated nuts in respect to drilled cotter pin holes in bolts.
notes.back: Give a smooth bearing surface, act as a shim for correct grip length, and position castellated nuts to cotter pin holes.

notes.front: When are lock washers used, and how do they work?
notes.explanation: Their use is barred in many places, such as primary or secondary structures and where exposed to airflow.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Lock Washers”, p. 7-46
notes.evidence: Lock washers, both the AN935 and AN936, are used with machine screws or bolts where the self-locking or castellatedtype nut is not appropriate. The spring action of the washer (AN935) provides enough friction to prevent loosening of the nut from vibration.
notes.back: With machine screws or bolts where a self-locking or castellated nut is not appropriate; their spring action gives friction against vibration.

notes.front: Where are ball socket and seat washers used?
notes.explanation: They are one of the special washer types, alongside washers for internal wrenching bolts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Special Washers”, p. 7-47
notes.evidence: The ball socket and seat washers, AC950 and AC955, are special washers used where a bolt is installed at an angle to a surface or where perfect alignment with a surface is required. These washers are used together.
notes.back: Together, where a bolt is installed at an angle to a surface or perfect alignment with a surface is needed.

notes.front: A steel bolt will secure two aluminium-alloy members. What washer does the handbook call for under the head and the nut?
notes.explanation: Any corrosion then attacks the washer rather than the aluminium members.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Installation Practices”, p. 7-48
notes.evidence: An aluminumalloy washer should be used under the head and nut of a steel bolt securing aluminum alloy or magnesium alloy members. Any corrosion that occurs attacks the washer rather than the members.
notes.back: D) An aluminium-alloy washer
notes.choices:
A) A cadmium-plated steel lock washer
B) A steel washer
C) No washer, to save weight
D) An aluminium-alloy washer
notes.choicesExplained: A: lock washers are barred from primary and secondary structure fasteners. C: washers are used under both heads and nuts unless omission is specified. B: steel washers are for steel members joined with steel bolts.

notes.front: Whenever possible, which way should a bolt be installed?
notes.explanation: That positioning tends to stop the bolt slipping out if the nut is accidentally lost.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Installation Practices”, p. 7-48
notes.evidence: Whenever possible, place the bolt with the head on top or in the forward position. This positioning tends to prevent the bolt from slipping out if the nut is
notes.back: Head on top or in the forward position.

notes.front: What is a bolt’s grip length, and how should it relate to the material?
notes.explanation: A slightly longer grip may be used with washers under the nut or head.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Installation Practices”, p. 7-48
notes.evidence: Grip length is the length of the unthreaded portion of the bolt shank. The grip length should equal the thickness of the material being bolted together. However, bolts of slightly greater grip length may be used if washers are placed under the nut or the bolt head.
notes.back: The length of the unthreaded shank; it should equal the thickness of the material being bolted.

notes.front: What is a Helicoil insert?
notes.explanation: It restores damaged internal threads and also protects tapped threads in light materials in original designs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Helicoils”, p. 7-49
notes.evidence: Helicoils are precision-formed screw thread coils of 18-8 stainless steel wire having a diamond-shaped cross section.
notes.back: A precision coil of 18-8 stainless steel wire with a diamond-shaped cross-section, used as a screw thread bushing.

notes.front: Why must proper torque be applied to all nuts, bolts, studs and screws?
notes.explanation: Structural members are more highly stressed as aircraft speed increases.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Fastener Torque”, p. 7-49
notes.evidence: It is therefore extremely important that each member carry no more and no less than the load for which it was designed. To distribute the loads safely throughout a structure, it is necessary that proper torque be applied to all nuts, bolts, studs, and screws.
notes.back: So each member carries no more and no less than its design load, the structure develops its designed strength, and fatigue failure is less likely.

notes.front: How does a Hi-Lok collar ensure the right preload without a torque check?
notes.explanation: This is why the fastener cannot be over-torqued.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “HI-LOK™ Fastening System”, p. 7-61
notes.evidence: This shear-off point occurs when a predetermined preload or clamp-up is attained in the fastener during installation.
notes.back: Its wrenching end shears off when a predetermined preload is reached, leaving the collar seated at the proper torque.

notes.front: In a Hi-Lok fastener installation, what is “preload”?
notes.explanation: The handbook defines preload for these fasteners as the maximum tensile load experienced during installation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “HI-LOK™ Fastening System”, p. 7-61
notes.evidence: For these fasteners, “Preload” is defined as the maximum tensile load experienced by a fastener in a joint during the fastener installation sequence.
notes.back: B) The maximum tensile load in the fastener during installation
notes.choices:
A) The torque value read on the wrench dial
B) The maximum tensile load in the fastener during installation
C) The shear load the joint carries in flight
D) The load left after the joint relaxes
notes.choicesExplained: A: preload is a load in the fastener, not a wrench reading. D: that is residual tension. C: preload is a tensile load reached during installation.

notes.front: How is torque read or set on a flexible beam torque wrench?
notes.explanation: The rigid frame type is read the same way; the ratchet type works by a preset release.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Torque Wrenches”, p. 7-49
notes.evidence: The three most commonly used torque wrenches are the flexible beam, rigid frame, and the ratchet types. [Figure 7-33] When using the flexible beam and the rigid frame torque wrenches, the torque value is read visually on a dial or scale mounted on the handle of the wrench.
notes.back: The torque value is read visually on a dial or scale mounted on the handle.

notes.front: How is torque read on a rigid frame torque wrench?
notes.explanation: The ratchet type differs: it is preset and releases when the torque is reached.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Torque Wrenches”, p. 7-49
notes.evidence: When using the flexible beam and the rigid frame torque wrenches, the torque value is read visually on a dial or scale mounted on the handle of the wrench.
notes.back: Visually, on a dial or scale mounted on the handle, as with the flexible beam type.

notes.front: How is torque read or set on a ratchet torque wrench?
notes.explanation: The flexible beam, rigid frame and ratchet types are the three most commonly used torque wrenches.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Torque Wrenches”, p. 7-49
notes.evidence: When the applied torque reaches the torque value indicated on the handle setting, the handle automatically releases or “breaks” and moves freely for a short distance.
notes.back: It is set on a micrometer-type scale, and the handle releases or “breaks” when that torque is reached.

notes.front: With a drive-end extension on a torque wrench, what formula gives the wrench reading?
notes.explanation: A drive-end extension on any type of wrench makes the formula mandatory, and force must be applied at the point the lengths were measured from.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Torque Wrenches (Figure 7-33)”, p. 7-51
notes.evidence: Formula for use with extensions Tw = Te x A B A = Lever length of wrench B = Lever length of wrench plus extension Te = Required torque on bolt Tw = Torque reading on wrench dial
notes.back: Tw = Te × A ÷ B, where A is the wrench lever length and B is that length plus the extension.

notes.front: A nut needs 240 inch-pounds. The ratchet torque wrench’s lever length is 10 inches, and a 2-inch drive-end extension is fitted. What should the wrench be set to?
notes.explanation: Tw = Te × A ÷ B = 240 × 10 ÷ 12 = 200; the longer lever means less reading gives the required torque.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Torque Wrenches”, p. 7-49
notes.evidence: The use of a drive end extension on any type of torque wrench makes the use of the formula mandatory. When applying the formula, force must be applied to the handle of the torque wrench at the point from which the measurements were taken.
notes.back: C) 200 inch-pounds
notes.choices:
A) 288 inch-pounds
B) 240 inch-pounds
C) 200 inch-pounds
D) 120 inch-pounds
notes.choicesExplained: B: an extension changes the reading needed, so the formula is mandatory. A: this multiplies by B ÷ A (12 ÷ 10) instead of A ÷ B. D: this divides the required torque by the extension length alone.

notes.front: Under the standard torque table rules, how are foot-pounds found, and when may nuts or bolts be lubricated?
notes.explanation: The table is a guide whenever maintenance procedures give no specific torque values.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Torque Tables”, p. 7-50
notes.evidence: 1. To obtain values in foot-pounds, divide inch-pounds by 12. 2. Do not lubricate nuts or bolts except for corrosionresistant steel parts or where specifically instructed to do so.
notes.back: Divide inch-pounds by 12. Lubricate only corrosion-resistant steel parts or where specifically instructed.

notes.front: Space around a fitting means a mechanic must tighten by turning the bolt head rather than the nut. What do the torque table rules say?
notes.explanation: Turning the head adds shank friction, so the rules move toward the high side of the range, never past the maximum.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Torque Tables”, p. 7-50
notes.evidence: 3. Always tighten by rotating the nut first if possible. When space considerations make it necessary to tighten by rotating the bolt head, approach the high side of the indicated torque range. Do not exceed the maximum allowable torque value.
notes.back: D) Approach the high side of the torque range without exceeding the maximum
notes.choices:
A) Use the low side of the range
B) Lubricate the threads to make up the difference
C) Double the table value
D) Approach the high side of the torque range without exceeding the maximum
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule is to approach the high side when turning the bolt head. C: the maximum allowable torque must not be exceeded. B: nuts and bolts are not lubricated except for corrosion-resistant steel or when instructed.

notes.front: If a castellated nut’s slots do not line up with the cotter pin hole within the recommended torque range, what does the handbook say to do?
notes.explanation: Safety wire holes follow the same principle: never over-torque or loosen a torqued nut to align them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cotter Pin Hole Line Up”, p. 7-50
notes.evidence: Except in cases of highly-stressed engine parts, the nut may not be over torque. Remove hardware and realign the holes.
notes.back: Do not over-torque (except on highly stressed engine parts); remove the hardware and realign the holes.

notes.front: At the top of the torque range, a castle nut’s slot is still a little short of the cotter pin hole on an airframe fitting. What should the mechanic do?
notes.explanation: The handbook’s rule is not to over-torque; realigning the hardware is the answer outside highly stressed engine parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cotter Pin Hole Line Up”, p. 7-50
notes.evidence: Except in cases of highly-stressed engine parts, the nut may not be over torque. Remove hardware and realign the holes.
notes.back: D) Remove the hardware and realign the holes
notes.choices:
A) Tighten past the range until the slot lines up
B) Back the nut off to the previous slot
C) Leave the cotter pin out
D) Remove the hardware and realign the holes
notes.choicesExplained: A: the nut may not be over-torqued except on highly stressed engine parts. B: loosening a torqued nut to align holes is not allowed. C: castellated nuts are used with drilled bolts precisely so they can be safetied.

notes.front: Which rivet head types are usually used where rivets are exposed to airflow, and which inside the structure?
notes.explanation: Four head designs almost completely replaced the many early designs as aircraft were standardised.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Aircraft Rivets”, p. 7-52
notes.evidence: Rivets exposed to the airflow over the top of the structure are usually either universal head MS20470 or 100° countersunk head MS20426 rivets. For rivets used in internal
notes.back: Outside: universal head MS20470 or 100° countersunk MS20426. Inside: roundhead MS20430 and flathead MS20442.

notes.front: Why must hardware store rivets never replace aircraft rivets?
notes.explanation: Aircraft countersunk heads use 100° for more surface contact to hold them in place.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Aircraft Rivets”, p. 7-51
notes.evidence: The rivets may be made from very different materials, the strength of the rivets differs greatly, and their shear strength qualities are very different. The countersunk heads on hardware store rivets are 78°, whereas countersunk aircraft rivets have 100° angle heads for more surface contact to hold it in place.
notes.back: Their materials and strength differ greatly, and their countersunk heads are 78° instead of aircraft 100°.

notes.front: A mechanic is riveting a magnesium-alloy structure. Which rivet alloy does the handbook give?
notes.explanation: 5056 is chosen for its corrosion-resistant qualities in combination with magnesium.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Solid Shank Rivets”, p. 7-52
notes.evidence: The 5056 rivet is used for riveting magnesium-alloy structures because of its corrosion-resistant qualities in combination with magnesium.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the field rivet is for aluminium alloy structures. B: this soft rivet is for nonstructural parts in soft aluminium alloys. C: copper rivets are only for copper alloys or nonmetallic materials such as leather.

notes.front: Which rivet alloy has the code A and is marked on the head with nothing (a plain head)?
notes.explanation: The 1100 rivet is very soft, for nonstructural parts where strength is not a factor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Figure 7-35. Rivet identification chart”, p. 7-55
notes.evidence: AD Recessed Dot 2117T 7075-T73 A Plain Head Marking 1100
notes.back: 1100 aluminium.

notes.front: Which rivet alloy has the code `AD` and is marked on the head with a recessed dot?
notes.explanation: It is used more than any other rivet for aluminium alloy structures and needs no heat-treatment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Figure 7-35. Rivet identification chart”, p. 7-55
notes.evidence: AD Recessed Dot 2117T 7075-T73 A Plain Head Marking 1100
notes.back: 2117-T aluminium: the field rivet.

notes.front: Which rivet alloy has the code D and is marked on the head with a raised dot?
notes.explanation: It is one of the two icebox rivet alloys.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Figure 7-35. Rivet identification chart”, p. 7-55
notes.evidence: D D DD B Raised Dot Raised Dot Raised Double Dash Raised Cross 2017T 2017T-HD 2024T 5056T
notes.back: 2017-T aluminium.

notes.front: Which rivet alloy has the code `DD` and is marked on the head with a raised double dash?
notes.explanation: It is one of the two icebox rivet alloys, and the one that must be driven soonest after leaving the refrigerator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Figure 7-35. Rivet identification chart”, p. 7-55
notes.evidence: D D DD B Raised Dot Raised Dot Raised Double Dash Raised Cross 2017T 2017T-HD 2024T 5056T
notes.back: 2024-T aluminium.

notes.front: Which rivet alloy has the code B and is marked on the head with a raised cross?
notes.explanation: It is used for magnesium-alloy structures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Figure 7-35. Rivet identification chart”, p. 7-55
notes.evidence: D D DD B Raised Dot Raised Dot Raised Double Dash Raised Cross 2017T 2017T-HD 2024T 5056T
notes.back: 5056 aluminium.

notes.front: A bin holds aluminium-alloy rivets whose heads carry a raised double dash. Which rivets are they, and how must they be handled?
notes.explanation: The raised double dash marks 2024-T, one of the heat-treatable alloys that age harden unless refrigerated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Figure 7-35. Rivet identification chart”, p. 7-55
notes.evidence: D D DD B Raised Dot Raised Dot Raised Double Dash Raised Cross 2017T 2017T-HD 2024T 5056T
notes.back: D) 2024-T icebox rivets, kept refrigerated until driven
notes.choices:
A) 1100 rivets for nonstructural parts
B) 2117-T field rivets, usable straight from the bin
C) 5056 rivets for magnesium structures
D) 2024-T icebox rivets, kept refrigerated until driven
notes.choicesExplained: B: field rivets carry a recessed dot. C: 5056 rivets carry a raised cross. A: 1100 rivets have a plain head.
