notes.front: In a rivet part number, how are shank diameter and length given?
notes.explanation: So a 3 before the dash means 3/32 inch diameter, and a 5 after it means 5/16 inch length.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification”, p. 7-56
notes.evidence: The first number following the material composition letters expresses the diameter of the rivet shank in 32nds of an inch. For example, 3 indicates 3⁄32, 5 indicates 5⁄32, and so forth. [Figure 7-38] The last number(s), separated by a dash from the preceding number, expresses the length of the rivet shank in 16ths of an inch.
notes.back: The first number after the material letters is the diameter in 32nds of an inch; the number after the dash is the length in 16ths.

notes.front: What rivet is `MS20470AD4-6`?
notes.explanation: The 470 is the universal head, `AD` is 2117-T, the 4 is 4/32 inch diameter and the 6 is 6/16 inch length.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Identification”, p. 7-56
notes.evidence: AN470AD3-5—complete part number AN—Air Force-Navy standard number 470—universal head rivet AN441—flathead rivets AD—2117-T aluminum alloy
notes.back: C) Universal head, 2117-T aluminium, 1/8 inch diameter, 3/8 inch long
notes.choices:
A) Countersunk head, 2024-T aluminium, 4/16 inch diameter, 6/32 inch long
B) Universal head, 2117-T aluminium, 4/32 inch long, 6/16 inch diameter
C) Universal head, 2117-T aluminium, 1/8 inch diameter, 3/8 inch long
D) Roundhead, 1100 aluminium, 1/8 inch diameter, 3/8 inch long
notes.choicesExplained: A: MS20470 is universal head, `AD` is 2117-T, and the units are reversed. B: the first number is the diameter and the dash number the length. D: roundhead is MS20430, and 1100 carries the code A.

notes.front: Where are blind rivets used instead of solid shank rivets?
notes.explanation: They are designed to be bucked from the front.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Blind Rivets”, p. 7-56
notes.evidence: There are many places on an aircraft where access to both sides of a riveted structure or structural part is impossible, or where limited space does not permit the use of a bucking bar.
notes.back: Where one side cannot be reached, space does not allow a bucking bar, or full solid-rivet strength is not needed.

notes.front: A blind rivet is to go into an area subject to considerable vibration. Which type is recommended?
notes.explanation: Its greater stem retention is why the handbook recommends it where there is considerable vibration.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Self-Plugging Rivets (Mechanical Lock)”, p. 7-59
notes.evidence: In addition, because of its greater stem retention characteristic, installation in areas subject to considerable vibration is recommended.
notes.back: D) A mechanical lock self-plugging rivet
notes.choices:
A) A friction lock self-plugging rivet
B) A pull-thru rivet
C) A hardware store pop rivet
D) A mechanical lock self-plugging rivet
notes.choicesExplained: A: vibration can make friction lock rivets loosen and fall out. B: pull-thru rivets are hollow after installation, with no locked stem. C: hardware store rivets must never replace aircraft rivets.

notes.front: Which turnlock fastener consists of a stud, grommet and receptacle and locks with a quarter turn clockwise?
notes.explanation: Its stud head shows the body diameter in sixteenths of an inch and the length in hundredths.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Dzus Fasteners”, p. 7-65
notes.evidence: A quarter of a turn of the stud (clockwise) locks the fastener. The fastener may be unlocked only by turning the stud counterclockwise. A Dzus key or a specially ground screwdriver locks or unlocks the fastener.
notes.back: The Dzus fastener.

notes.front: Which turnlock fastener has a heavy-duty stressed panel version and is used to secure cowlings and fairings?
notes.explanation: Its stud and grommet go in the removable part, and the receptacle is riveted to the aircraft structure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Camloc Fasteners”, p. 7-65
notes.evidence: The latter is used in stressed panels, which carry structural loads. The Camloc fastener is used to secure aircraft cowlings and
notes.back: The Camloc fastener.

notes.front: Which turnlock fastener uses a stud, a cross pin and a stud receptacle, with a cross pin that must never be reused?
notes.explanation: Once removed from the stud, the chrome-vanadium cross pin is replaced with a new one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Airloc Fasteners”, p. 7-66
notes.evidence: The Airloc fastener consists of three parts: a stud, a cross pin, and a stud receptacle.
notes.back: The Airloc fastener.

notes.front: A Dzus stud is marked F 6½ 0.50. What do the figures mean?
notes.explanation: Dzus diameter is always measured in sixteenths of an inch and length in hundredths.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Dzus Fasteners”, p. 7-65
notes.evidence: The diameter is always measured in sixteenths of an inch. Stud length is measured in hundredths of an inch and is the distance from the head of the stud to the bottom of the spring hole.
notes.back: D) Flush head, 6½/16 inch body diameter, 0.50 inch long
notes.choices:
A) Flush head, 6½ mm diameter, 50 mm long
B) Oval head, 6½/16 inch long, 0.50 inch diameter
C) Flush head, 6½/32 inch diameter, 0.50 inch long
D) Flush head, 6½/16 inch body diameter, 0.50 inch long
notes.choicesExplained: A: diameter is in sixteenths of an inch and length in hundredths of an inch. B: F means flush, and the order is diameter then length. C: Dzus diameter is always in sixteenths, not 32nds.

notes.front: In the handbook’s four groups of commonly used screws, what is the first group?
notes.explanation: They are alloy steel, heat-treated, and can be used as structural bolts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Screws”, p. 7-66
notes.evidence: 1. Structural screws, which have the same strength as equal size bolts. 2. Machine screws, which include most types used for general repair.
notes.back: Structural screws, with the same strength as equal-size bolts.

notes.front: In the handbook’s four groups of commonly used screws, what is the second group?
notes.explanation: They come in flathead, roundhead and washer head types.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Screws”, p. 7-66
notes.evidence: 1. Structural screws, which have the same strength as equal size bolts. 2. Machine screws, which include most types used for general repair.
notes.back: Machine screws, including most types used for general repair.

notes.front: In the handbook’s four groups of commonly used screws, what is the third group?
notes.explanation: They cut their own threads and must not replace standard screws, nuts, bolts or rivets.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Screws”, p. 7-66
notes.evidence: 3. Self-tapping screws, which are used for attaching lighter parts. 4. Drive screws, which are not actually screws but nails.
notes.back: Self-tapping screws, used for attaching lighter parts.

notes.front: In the handbook’s four groups of commonly used screws, what is the fourth group?
notes.explanation: Their heads are not slotted or recessed, and they are not meant to be removed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Screws”, p. 7-66
notes.evidence: 3. Self-tapping screws, which are used for attaching lighter parts. 4. Drive screws, which are not actually screws but nails.
notes.back: Drive screws: not really screws but nails, driven in with a mallet or hammer.

notes.front: A mechanic wants to replace a missing structural bolt with a self-tapping sheet metal screw because it fits the hole. Is this acceptable?
notes.explanation: Self-tapping screws attach lighter parts and cut their own threads; the handbook forbids them as replacements for standard fasteners.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Self-Tapping Screws”, p. 7-67
notes.evidence: They are used in the temporary attachment of metal for riveting, and in the permanent assembly of nonstructural assemblies. Self-tapping screws should not be used to replace standard screws, nuts, bolts, or rivets.
notes.back: A) No; self-tapping screws must not replace standard screws, nuts, bolts or rivets
notes.choices:
A) No; self-tapping screws must not replace standard screws, nuts, bolts or rivets
B) Yes, if it is torqued to the bolt’s value
C) Yes, because all screws have bolt strength
D) Yes, for a temporary repair in flight-critical structure
notes.choicesExplained: B: the prohibition does not depend on torque. C: only structural screws match the strength of equal-size bolts. D: self-tapping sheet metal screws are for temporary attachment during riveting and nonstructural assemblies.

notes.front: What is 7 × 7 control cable, and where is it used?
notes.explanation: Six strands are laid around a centre strand, and fewer wires per strand make it less flexible than 7 × 19.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cable Construction”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: The 7 × 7 cable consists of seven strands of seven wires each. Six of these
notes.back: Seven strands of seven wires: medium flexibility, for trim tab, engine and indicator controls.

notes.front: What is 7 × 19 control cable, and where is it used?
notes.explanation: Its greater flexibility suits frequent operation over pulleys.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cable Construction”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: The 7 × 19 cable is made up of seven strands of 19 wires each. Six of these strands are laid around the center strand. [Figure 7-68] This cable is extra flexible and is used in primary control systems and in other places where operation over pulleys is frequent.
notes.back: Seven strands of 19 wires: extra flexible, for primary controls and where cables run often over pulleys.

notes.front: A new trim tab control run is being fitted. Which cable construction does the handbook associate with trim tab controls?
notes.explanation: The 7 × 7 cable’s medium flexibility is matched to trim tab, engine and indicator controls.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cable Construction”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: This is a cable of medium flexibility and is used for trim tab controls, engine controls, and indicator controls.
notes.back: B) 7 × 7, medium flexibility
notes.choices:
A) 7 × 19, extra flexible
B) 7 × 7, medium flexibility
C) 3 × 7, the smallest size
D) A push-pull tube is required
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is for primary controls and runs often over pulleys. C: the handbook names 7 × 7 and 7 × 19 as the most common aircraft cables. D: trim tab controls are a stated use of cable.

notes.front: At an annual or 100-hour inspection, when must a control cable assembly be replaced for broken wires?
notes.explanation: Wire breakage is easy to see, but wear, corrosion and distortion are not, so cables are also removed periodically for closer inspection.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-149, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: a. At each annual or 100-hour inspection, all control cables must be inspected for broken wires strands. Any cable assembly that has one broken wire strand located in a critical fatigue area must be replaced.
notes.back: When it has one broken wire strand in a critical fatigue area.

notes.front: What counts as a critical fatigue area on a control cable?
notes.explanation: Swaging pressures can pinch small wires, which then fail early near the fitting.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-149, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: b. A critical fatigue area is defined as the working length of a cable where the cable runs over, under, or around a pulley, sleeve, or through a fair-lead; any section where the cable is flexed, rubbed, or worked in any manner; or any point within 1 foot of a swaged-on fitting.
notes.back: Where it runs over, under or around a pulley, sleeve or fairlead; where flexed or rubbed; or within 1 foot of a swaged-on fitting.

notes.front: Checking a cable where it passes over a pulley, a mechanic suspects a broken wire that is not sticking out. What does the advisory circular recommend?
notes.explanation: A broken wire will not always protrude, so the cloth, a careful visual check and magnification are used together.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-149, p. 7-39
notes.evidence: If a broken wire of this type is suspected, further inspection with a magnifying glass of 7 power or greater is recommended.
notes.back: D) Pass a cloth over it, inspect closely, and use a magnifier of 7 power or more
notes.choices:
A) Run a bare hand along the cable to feel for wires
B) Accept it, since a broken wire always protrudes
C) Increase the cable tension and recheck
D) Pass a cloth over it, inspect closely, and use a magnifier of 7 power or more
notes.choicesExplained: A: the method given is a cloth that snags on broken wires. B: a broken wire may lie in the strand and show only as a hairline crack. C: tension adjustment does not find broken wires.

notes.front: Why is a flathead (clevis) pin customarily installed head up?
notes.explanation: Flathead pins are used with tie rod terminals and in secondary controls not in continuous operation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Flathead Pin”, p. 7-75
notes.evidence: The pin is customarily installed with the head up so that if the cotter pin fails or works out, the pin remains in place.
notes.back: So that if the cotter pin fails or works out, the pin stays in place.

notes.front: Which safety wiring method is the most common?
notes.explanation: The single wire method is kept for particular cases such as closely spaced patterns and electrical parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Nuts, Bolts, & Screws”, p. 7-77
notes.evidence: Nuts, bolts, and screws are safety wired by the single wire or double twist method. The double twist method is the most common method of safety wiring.
notes.back: The double twist method.

notes.front: Where may the single wire method of safety wiring be used?
notes.explanation: Double twist is the default; single wire suits these particular cases.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Nuts, Bolts, & Screws”, p. 7-77
notes.evidence: The single wire method may be used on small screws in a closely spaced closed geometrical pattern, on parts in electrical systems, and in places that are extremely difficult to reach.
notes.back: On small screws in a closely spaced closed geometrical pattern, on parts in electrical systems, and in places very hard to reach.

notes.front: A mechanic is safety wiring widely spaced bolts in series with the double twist method. What is the most that should be wired in one series?
notes.explanation: The number depends on the application; for widely spaced bolts by the double twist method, three is the maximum.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Nuts, Bolts, & Screws”, p. 7-77
notes.evidence: For instance, when safety wiring widely spaced bolts by the double twist method, a group of three should be the maximum number in a series.
notes.back: B) Three
notes.choices:
A) Two
B) Three
C) Six
D) As many as a 24-inch wire reaches
notes.choicesExplained: A: two is allowed, but the stated maximum for widely spaced bolts is a group of three. D: that limit is for closely spaced bolts. C: that exceeds the group of three given for widely spaced bolts.

notes.front: In which direction must safety wire pull?
notes.explanation: Parts are torqued and the holes aligned before safetying.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Nuts, Bolts, & Screws”, p. 7-77
notes.evidence: The wire is arranged so that if the bolt or screw begins to loosen, the force applied to the wire is in the tightening direction. Parts being safety wired should be torqued to recommend values and the holes aligned before attempting the safetying operation.
notes.back: In the tightening direction, so that if the fastener begins to loosen the wire pulls it tighter.

notes.front: Under the general safety wiring rules, can safety wire be reused, and how is the pigtail finished?
notes.explanation: Bending the pigtail back or under stops it becoming a snag.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “General Safety Wiring Rules”, p. 7-80
notes.evidence: 1. Pigtail of 1⁄4 to 1⁄2 inch (three to six twists) should be made at the end of the wiring. This pigtail must be bent back or under to prevent it from becoming a snag. 2. The safety wire must be new upon each application.
notes.back: No; wire must be new each time. The pigtail is 1/4 to 1/2 inch (three to six twists), bent back or under.

notes.front: A castellated nut is to be safety wired, but at the selected torque its slot does not line up with the hole. What do the rules say?
notes.explanation: Starting at the low side of the range leaves room to reach a slot without over-torquing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “General Safety Wiring Rules”, p. 7-80
notes.evidence: 3. When castellated nuts are to be secured with safety wire, tighten the nut to the low side of the selected torque range, unless otherwise specified, and if necessary, continue tightening until a slot aligns with the hole.
notes.back: C) Tighten to the low side of the torque range, then continue if needed until a slot aligns
notes.choices:
A) Use the old wire, twisted tighter
B) Back the nut off until a slot aligns
C) Tighten to the low side of the torque range, then continue if needed until a slot aligns
D) Route the wire so it pulls in the loosening direction
notes.choicesExplained: B: never loosen a torqued nut to align safety wire holes. A: safety wire must be new upon each application. D: all pull exerted by the wire must tend to tighten the nut.

notes.front: According to Advisory Circular 43.13-1B, is safetying a means of obtaining or keeping torque?
notes.explanation: Safetying secures parts so vibration will not loosen them; torque is set separately.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-122, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: These practices are not a means of obtaining or maintaining torque, rather a safety device to prevent the disengagement of screws, nuts, bolts, snap rings, oil caps, drain cocks, valves, and parts.
notes.back: No. It is a safety device to prevent screws, nuts, bolts and other parts from disengaging.

notes.front: A mechanic is safetying a fire extinguisher handle guard that must break free in an emergency. Which safety wire does the advisory circular call for?
notes.explanation: Emergency operation may depend on the wire shearing, so strong wires are barred and thin copper or brass is used.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-123, p. 7-18
notes.evidence: Do not use stainless steel, Monel, carbon steel, or aluminum alloy safety wire to secure emergency mechanisms such as switch handles, guards covering handles used on exits, fire extinguishers, emergency gear releases, or other emergency equipment.
notes.back: A) Copper or brass wire of .020-inch diameter where the equipment requires it
notes.choices:
A) Copper or brass wire of .020-inch diameter where the equipment requires it
B) Stainless steel wire, for strength
C) Monel wire, for corrosion resistance
D) .032-inch carbon steel wire
notes.choicesExplained: B: stainless steel must not be used on emergency mechanisms. C: Monel is also barred from emergency mechanisms. D: carbon steel is barred from emergency mechanisms.

notes.front: How far must turnbuckle terminals be screwed into the barrel?
notes.explanation: Both terminals are screwed in an equal number of turns when the turnbuckle is installed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Turnbuckles”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: It is also essential that all turnbuckle terminals be screwed into the barrel until not more than three threads are exposed on either side of the turnbuckle barrel.
notes.back: Until no more than three threads are exposed on either side of the barrel.

notes.front: After adjusting a cable turnbuckle, a mechanic sees five threads showing on one terminal and one on the other. What is wrong?
notes.explanation: Both terminals go in an equal number of turns, with no more than three threads exposed at either side.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Turnbuckles”, p. 7-72
notes.evidence: When installing a turnbuckle in a control system, it is necessary to screw both terminals an equal number of turns into the barrel.
notes.back: D) The terminals are unequal, and more than three threads show on one side
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as long as total thread showing is six
B) Only the side with one thread showing is wrong
C) Nothing, if it is safetied with the double wrap method
D) The terminals are unequal, and more than three threads show on one side
notes.choicesExplained: A: no more than three may show on either side. B: one thread is within the limit; five is not. C: safetying does not correct incorrect thread engagement.

notes.front: Of the safety wire methods for turnbuckles, which does Advisory Circular 43.13-1B prefer, and may safety wire be reused?
notes.explanation: Single-wrap methods are acceptable but not the equal of double wrap.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 7-179 and 7-180, p. 7-49
notes.evidence: Do not reuse safety wire. Adjust the turnbuckle to the correct cable tension so that no more than three cable threads are exposed on either side of the turnbuckle barrel. 7-180. DOUBLE-WRAP METHOD. Of the methods using safety wire for safetying turnbuckles, the method described here is preferred,
notes.back: The double-wrap method; safety wire must not be reused.

notes.front: In cotter pin safetying, how far may the prong bent over the bolt end extend, and where must the downward prong not rest?
notes.explanation: Prongs are cut off if necessary, and all bends use a reasonable radius since sharp bends invite breakage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cotter Pin Safetying”, p. 7-80
notes.evidence: 1. The prong bent over the bolt end should not extend beyond the bolt diameter. (Cut it off if necessary.) 2. The prong bent down should not rest against the surface of the washer. (Again, cut it off if necessary.)
notes.back: Not beyond the bolt diameter; the downward prong must not rest against the washer surface.

notes.front: A mechanic is bending cotter pin prongs over a castellated nut. What is the best method, according to the handbook?
notes.explanation: Sharp angled bends invite breakage, so gentle mallet taps give the needed radius.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 7, “Cotter Pin Safetying”, p. 7-80
notes.evidence: 4. All prongs should be bent over a reasonable radius. Sharp angled bends invite breakage. Tapping lightly with a mallet is the best method of bending the prongs.
notes.back: B) Tap lightly with a mallet, bending over a reasonable radius
notes.choices:
A) Bend sharply with pliers for a tight fit
B) Tap lightly with a mallet, bending over a reasonable radius
C) Spread the prongs outward from the sides of the nut
D) Leave the prongs straight
notes.choicesExplained: A: sharp angled bends invite breakage. D: the prongs are bent over the bolt end and down the nut. C: in the wraparound method the prongs must not extend outward from the sides.

notes.front: What are soft solders chiefly made of, and at what temperature does 50/50 solder melt?
notes.explanation: It is the general purpose solder and the one most frequently used.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-88(4)(e), p. 4-74
notes.evidence: Half-and-half (50/50) solder is a general purpose solder and is most frequently used. It contains equal proportions of tin and lead, and it melts at approximately 182 ºC (360 ºF).
notes.back: Tin and lead; half-and-half (50/50) melts at approximately 360 °F.

notes.front: Why must soft solder never join structural members?
notes.explanation: It should be used only where transmitted loads are very low.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-88(4)(a), p. 4-74
notes.evidence: (a) Soft solder gradually yields under a steadily applied load and should not be used unless the transmitted loads are very low. It should never be used as a means of joining structural members.
notes.back: It gradually yields under a steadily applied load.

notes.front: Before a silver-brazed or soldered joint is made, the parts are cleaned to bright metal. What does the flux then do during the operation?
notes.explanation: Any film of oxide stops the filler contacting the base metal, so flux keeps the metal chemically clean.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-88(2)(c), p. 4-73
notes.evidence: During the soldering operation, the flux continues the process of keeping oxide away from the metal and aids the flow of solder.
notes.back: C) Keeps oxide away from the metal and aids the flow of solder
notes.choices:
A) Lowers the melting point of the base metal
B) Adds strength to the finished joint
C) Keeps oxide away from the metal and aids the flow of solder
D) Replaces the need to clean the joint
notes.choicesExplained: B: flux acts on oxide and flow, not joint strength. A: the base metal is not melted in soldering or brazing. D: the joint must first be physically and chemically clean.

notes.front: Which form of arc welding fills most needs in aircraft maintenance?
notes.explanation: Its electrode is a tungsten rod, and inert gas such as argon or helium shields the arc from oxides.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-86d, p. 4-69
notes.evidence: d. Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW). This is the form of electric arc welding that fills most of the needs in aircraft maintenance. It is more commonly known as tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding.
notes.back: Gas tungsten arc welding, commonly called tungsten inert gas welding.

notes.front: On a tungsten inert gas welder, what current is set for aluminium and magnesium, and what for mild steel, stainless steel and titanium?
notes.explanation: Metals with refractory surface oxide films, such as aluminium and magnesium, are generally welded with alternating current.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-86d, p. 4-69
notes.evidence: FIGURE 4-29. SET TIG WELDER TO DC CURRENT, STRAIGHT POLARITY FOR WELDING MILD STEEL, STAINLESS STEEL, AND TITANIUM
notes.back: Alternating current for aluminium and magnesium; direct current, straight polarity, for the steels and titanium.

notes.front: A shop will produce large volumes of welded parts using an uncoated wire electrode fed through the torch with a shielding gas. Which process is this?
notes.explanation: Gas metal arc welding feeds uncoated wire with inert gas around it and is used more for large-volume production than for aircraft repair.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-86c, p. 4-68
notes.evidence: c. Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW). This method of welding was formerly called Metal Inert Gas (MIG) welding,
notes.back: D) Gas metal arc welding (formerly metal inert gas)
notes.choices:
A) Gas tungsten arc welding
B) Oxyacetylene gas welding
C) Shielded metal arc (stick) welding
D) Gas metal arc welding (formerly metal inert gas)
notes.choicesExplained: A: its electrode is a non-consumable tungsten rod, with filler fed by hand. C: stick welding uses a flux-coated rod, not an uncoated fed wire. B: gas welding uses a fuel-gas flame, not an electric arc.

notes.front: What does a good weld look like, according to the handbook?
notes.explanation: Appearance is not a positive indication of quality, but it is a good clue to the care used in making the weld.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 10, “Inspection of Welds”, p. 10-38
notes.evidence: A good weld is uniform in width; the ripples are even and well feathered into the base metal and show no burn due to overheating. [Figure 10-38] The weld has good penetration and is free of gas pockets, porosity, or inclusions.
notes.back: Uniform in width, with even ripples well feathered into the base metal, no overheating burn, good penetration and no gas pockets, porosity or inclusions.

notes.front: How much penetration should a butt weld and a fillet weld have?
notes.explanation: Penetration is the depth of fusion, and thorough fusion is the most important characteristic of a sound weld.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 10, “Inspection of Welds”, p. 10-38
notes.evidence: In a butt weld, the penetration should be 100 percent of the thickness of the base metal. On a fillet weld, the penetration requirements are 25 to 50 percent of the thickness of the base metal.
notes.back: Butt weld: 100 percent of base metal thickness. Fillet weld: 25 to 50 percent.

notes.front: Inspecting a finished steel weld, a mechanic finds oxide on the base metal 1 inch from the weld. Under Advisory Circular 43.13-1B, is this acceptable?
notes.explanation: A completed weld is checked visually against a list that includes no oxide more than 1/2 inch from the weld.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-78, p. 4-65
notes.evidence: c. No oxide has formed on the base metal more than 1/2 inch from the weld. d. There are no signs of blowholes, porosity, or projecting globules.
notes.back: A) No; oxide should not have formed more than 1/2 inch from the weld
notes.choices:
A) No; oxide should not have formed more than 1/2 inch from the weld
B) Yes, if it is ground off smooth
C) Yes, oxide is normal anywhere on a gas weld
D) Yes, as long as there is no porosity
notes.choicesExplained: C: the visual criteria limit oxide to within 1/2 inch. B: filing or grinding welds causes a loss of strength and is not the check. D: each visual criterion must be met, not just one.

notes.front: What does a weld with long, pointed ripples show?
notes.explanation: Cross-sectioned, such a weld would probably show gas pockets, porosity and slag inclusions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 10, “Inspection of Welds”, p. 10-38
notes.evidence: The weld in Figure 10-38A was made too rapidly. The long and pointed appearance of the ripples was caused by an excessive amount of heat or an oxidizing flame.
notes.back: It was made too rapidly; the ripples come from excessive heat or an oxidising flame.

notes.front: What causes a weld with improper penetration and cold laps, rough and irregular with edges not feathered in?
notes.explanation: Without enough heat the filler does not fuse into the base metal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 10, “Inspection of Welds”, p. 10-38
notes.evidence: Figure 10-38B illustrates a weld that has improper penetration and cold laps caused by insufficient heat. It appears rough and irregular, and its edges are not feathered into the base metal.
notes.back: Insufficient heat.

notes.front: To make a lumpy weld bead look smooth, a mechanic proposes to file it flush and fill low spots with solder. What does the advisory circular say?
notes.explanation: Smoothing a weld by filing or grinding causes a loss of strength, and fillers are banned.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-81, p. 4-66
notes.evidence: Do not file or grind welds in an effort to create a smooth appearance, as such treatment causes a loss of strength. Do not fill welds with solder, brazing metal, or any other filler.
notes.back: D) Do neither: filing or grinding loses strength, and welds must not be filled with solder
notes.choices:
A) Filing is fine if solder fills the low spots
B) Grinding is fine if followed by painting
C) Fill with brazing metal instead of solder
D) Do neither: filing or grinding loses strength, and welds must not be filled with solder
notes.choicesExplained: A: both practices are listed among those to guard against. B: grinding to smooth appearance causes a loss of strength. C: welds are not to be filled with solder, brazing metal or any other filler.

notes.front: What standard must a weld repair on a flight-critical part meet, and what must be identified first?
notes.explanation: The advisory circular calls identifying these of utmost importance.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-74, p. 4-63
notes.evidence: When repairs of any of these flight-critical parts are required, it is extremely important to make the weld repairs equal to the original weld. Identifying the kind of metal to be welded, identifying the kind of welding process used in building the part originally, and determining the best way to make welded repairs are of utmost importance.
notes.back: It must equal the original weld; identify the metal, the original welding process, and the best repair method.

notes.front: Before rewelding a previously welded joint, what must be done, and what joints must never be welded?
notes.explanation: Welding over a weld reheats the material, which may make it lose strength and become brittle.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-81, p. 4-66
notes.evidence: When it is necessary to weld a joint which was previously welded, remove all of the old weld material before rewelding. Avoid welding over a weld, because reheating may cause the material to lose its strength and become brittle. Never weld a joint which has been previously brazed.
notes.back: Remove all the old weld material; never weld a joint that has been brazed.

notes.front: A cracked 7075 aluminium landing-gear attachment fitting is found. A mechanic suggests welding it. What does the advisory circular say?
notes.explanation: The circular lists 2024 and 7075 aluminium among aircraft parts not to be welded.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-89d, p. 4-75
notes.evidence: d. Nos. 2024 and 7075 Aluminum. Do not weld these two aluminum alloys (that are often used in aircraft construction) because the heat from the welding process will
notes.back: B) Do not weld 2024 or 7075; welding heat causes severe cracking
notes.choices:
A) Weld it with gas tungsten arc welding
B) Do not weld 2024 or 7075; welding heat causes severe cracking
C) Braze it instead
D) Weld it, then heat-treat to specifications
notes.choicesExplained: A: the ban on welding 7075 applies whatever the process. C: brazing is not used for structural repairs. D: heat-treating after welding is for weldable heat-treated steel members, not 7075.

notes.front: How far should an acetylene cylinder valve be opened?
notes.explanation: Keeping the cylinder wrench on the valve lets the cylinder be turned off quickly.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-114, p. 4-95
notes.evidence: DO NOT open an acetylene cylinder valve more than approximately 1-1/2 turns and preferably no more than 3/4 of a turn. Keep the cylinder wrench, if one is required, on the cylinder valve so, if necessary, the cylinder may be turned off quickly.
notes.back: No more than about 1½ turns, and preferably no more than ¾ of a turn.

notes.front: What lens shades does the advisory circular give for gas welding and for arc welding?
notes.explanation: Gas welding aluminium calls for cobalt-blue lenses instead.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B CHG 1, par. 4-115, p. 4-95
notes.evidence: (1) For gas welding and brazing, use number 3 or 4 green-shaded tempered lenses. (2) When gas welding aluminum, use cobalt-blue tint lenses. (3) When arc welding, including TIG, MIG, and plasma cutting; use number 9 to 12 green lenses and a full face-and-neck covering helmet.
notes.back: Gas welding and brazing: number 3 or 4 green. Arc welding: number 9 to 12 green with a full face-and-neck helmet.

notes.front: Of the four types of aircraft parts the handbook describes, which two are suspected unapproved parts?
notes.explanation: Good parts with good paperwork are approved; bad parts with bad paperwork are unapproved and must never be installed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 2, “Suspected Unapproved Parts (SUP)”, p. 2-24
notes.evidence: There are four types of aircraft parts: 1. Good parts with good paperwork. 2. Good parts with bad paperwork. 3. Bad parts with “good” (bogus) paperwork. 4. Bad parts with bad paperwork.
notes.back: Good parts with bad paperwork, and bad parts with “good” (bogus) paperwork.

notes.front: A mechanic receives a batch of bolts whose certificates do not match the part markings. What should happen to the bolts first?
notes.explanation: Suspected unapproved parts are segregated and quarantined; contacting the manufacturer is a good way to start gathering facts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), ch. 2, “Suspected Unapproved Parts (SUP)”, p. 2-24
notes.evidence: Suspected unapproved parts (SUPs) should be segregated and quarantined until proper disposition can be determined. Contacting the manufacturer of the product is a good way to start gathering the facts concerning the product in question.
notes.back: D) Segregate and quarantine them until disposition is determined
notes.choices:
A) Install them if they pass a visual check
B) Return them to general stock for later use
C) Throw them away quietly
D) Segregate and quarantine them until disposition is determined
notes.choicesExplained: A: questionable paperwork makes them suspected unapproved parts, whatever they look like. C: the handbook calls for quarantine and gathering facts, starting with the manufacturer. B: they must be kept apart until proper disposition is determined.
